docs.title: HQL
docs.text:
HQL, the Hyper Query Language, is a statically typed expression and query language. It combines functional expressions with pipelines over files, streams, structured data and HyperMarkDown documents, and checks a program's types before it evaluates it.

type Book { title : String, year : Int, rating : Int }

books = [
    Book(title = "Dune", year = 1965, rating = 5),
    Book(title = "Emma", year = 1815, rating = 3),
    Book(title = "Beloved", year = 1987, rating = 4),
]

books
| filter(b => b.rating >= 4)
| sort(b => b.title)
| map(b => b.title)

["Beloved", "Dune"]

source reads the documents a file holds, and target writes a value to one:

source(file("sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| target(file("morning.json"))
  • Install — a release binary or cargo install hql.
  • Learn HQL — the book in three parts, the language, data flows, and knowledge and AI, one runnable program at a time.
  • Reference — the grammar, the command line, and reporting.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The example corpus is where HQL's features are designed: an example is written first, and the implementation is held to it. Each query file declares its expected type and result in a header, and the test suite runs every one.

Corpus What it shows tutorial The reading-club vault the HQL book runs against: books, authors, their links, a relation card, an agent card and an embedding index for the questions the book asks notebook A reading list whose cells share values by id, built with hql render, and a meeting note whose cells run an agent over the draft, written as design birds Linked cards with runnable collection queries: repeated sightings, distinct species, keyed counts, ordered routes and sorted keys — plus intentional errors for duplicate keys and non-orderable sorted-map keys mapreduce Book cards filtered, grouped and reduced, read as a chain of steps functions Declared, generic and aliased functions, partial application, and intentional errors streams Generators with yield, an unbounded stream ended by take, and the lazy steps

docs.title: Reading a query header
docs.text:
// status: valid-now
// feature: Bird cards filtered and sorted by name
// implementation: implemented
// vault: birds/wiki
// expected-type: Seq<String>
// expected: ["Barn owl", "Common raven", "European robin"]

A header may instead say status: proposed with implementation: pending and a proposal: naming the record that specifies it. Such a case is a design input, pinned before it runs, and the suite asserts that it does not check yet — the day it does, it has to be promoted.

docs.title: Running one
docs.text:
From a clone, after cargo build --locked:

target/debug/hql --vault examples/birds/wiki run examples/birds/queries/catalog.hql

docs.title: From a release
docs.text:
Each release ships a binary for every supported target, with a checksum beside it. Download the pair from the releases page, check it, and put hql somewhere on your PATH:

shasum -a 256 -c hql-<version>-<target>.tar.gz.sha256   # sha256sum -c on Linux
tar -xzf hql-<version>-<target>.tar.gz

The targets are x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and x86_64-apple-darwin. Verify the archive against the published SHA-256 checksum before extracting it.

docs.title: With Cargo
docs.text:
With Rust 1.95 or newer from rustup:

cargo install hql --locked                                   # the last release
cargo install --git https://github.com/ewiger/hql --locked   # the latest commit
cargo install --path . --locked                              # from a clone

docs.title: Check it works
docs.text:
hql eval '40 + 2'

42

hql builtins lists every step a pipeline may use, grouped by the extension that provides it.

Versions

While the major version is 0, a minor release may change the language incompatibly. The changelog lists each such change by release.

docs.title: Learn HQL
docs.text:
This is a book about HQL, read from the first page to the last. It starts with a number and ends with a web of vaults, and every chapter builds on the ones before it. Every program in it prints what the book shows. Chapter 15 and chapters 20 to 22 describe ETL pipelines, the ai module and the direction beyond one vault, which are design and not in the current release; every other chapter runs with it.

HQL is a statically typed language for querying, transforming, connecting and computing over data, knowledge and AI workflows. A program is checked before it runs, and values flow through pipelines of typed steps: over records and lists, as jq works over JSON; over tables, as SQL does; over files, standard input and streams that do not end; over a vault of Markdown documents, their links and their meaning; and through the context, prompts and runs of a language model.

The book is in three parts. The language is the steps, the values they pass and the types that join them, from the first expression to the type system and the boundary where data from outside becomes typed. Data flows is the pipeline those steps form: what | does, when a program is checked, where it runs, and the systems a pipeline connects. Knowledge and AI is a vault of documents as a namespace, its graph, retrieval by meaning, documents that compute themselves, agents whose runs are values, documents that run them, and the web they point at.

docs.title: Following along
docs.text:
Install hql, clone the repository for the tutorial vault, and run each program with hql eval:

git clone https://github.com/ewiger/hql && cd hql
hql --vault examples/tutorial eval 'cards | size'

The tutorial vault, examples/tutorial/, is a small reading club: seven books, five authors, the links between them, one claim about which book inspired which, and a librarian.

docs.title: Part I: The language
docs.text:
1. Hello world — the first program, running it, and the check before a program runs.
  2. Data types — Int, Float, String and Bool in the REPL, Data and its JSON-shaped trees, Option for a value that may be missing, and how sets, Data and maps differ.
  3. Collections — lists, sets and maps, and the steps they share.
  4. Functions — lambdas, declared functions, the two body forms = expr and { … }, generic functions, aliases, and partial application.
  5. Modules — modules of your own, imports, receiver modules, public and private declarations, and how a name resolves.
  6. SQL-like Queries — where, order by, group by and the aggregates.
  7. Streams that do not end — generators, laziness, and batches.
  8. Writing results out — presentation formats and who chooses them.
  9. I/O — sources and targets: endpoints, source, tap, target and sink, finite or live, formats, sources by id and the schema boundary, channels, logging, the network, and hql as a command-line data tool.
  10. The type system — records, unions and match, results, subtypes and narrowing, generics, receiver calls, operators and traits.
  11. Advanced data typing — the type boundary where loose data becomes typed, open and closed types, TypeContract and DataContract, validators, validation as a value, and what a contract states that a schema cannot.
  12. Errors — failures kept as data, diagnostics and the run's diagnostic channel, strict and collect.
  13. Working with hql — the commands, the reports, and what to do when something is wrong.

docs.title: Part II: Data flows
docs.text:
1. Pipelines — | against ., the three phases, the step as the unit of execution, hql in a shell pipe, and the systems a pipeline will connect: queues, databases, services and jobs.
  2. ETL pipelines — one file that reads a queue, enriches from a database and writes tables, alerts and an archive: ids bound in configuration and how they break, streams against tables, a batch as a stream and a stream as a file, rejected rows as a source, and what each platform's wiring finds out when.

docs.title: Part III: Knowledge and AI
docs.text:
1. A vault of documents — cards, their metadata, a reading list nobody maintains, and the vault as a namespace.
  2. Links and graphs — following links, building graphs, drawing them.
  3. Finding cards by meaning — rankings, hits, and the evidence behind a score.
  4. Queries inside documents — cells, documents built from them, and cells that maintain a vault.
  5. Agents and runs — agents as cards, context and prompts, tools, and runs kept as values.
  6. Agents inside documents — a document whose cells retrieve evidence, run an agent over the draft they sit in, and remember the answer.
  7. The hyper web — namespaces beyond one tree, providers, retrieval and agents across them, and a reader who asks.

docs.title: 1. Hello world
docs.text: HQL is a statically typed expression and query language. A program is an expression, or a few statements ending in one; hql checks its type, then evaluates it, and writes the value. This chapter is about that loop.

docs.title: Hello, world
docs.text:
The smallest program that says hello is the text itself:

"Hello, world!"

"Hello, world!"

A program is an expression, and its value is what hql writes. fmt writes values into a template, one {} each:

fmt("Hello, {}!", "world")

"Hello, world!"

docs.title: Running a program
docs.text:
hql eval takes a program as an argument:

hql eval '"Hello, world!"'

Every program in this book runs that way. Most of them run against the tutorial vault, a small reading club in examples/tutorial/, so the commands in later chapters start with hql --vault examples/tutorial eval. The book shows each program in an hql block and what hql writes in the block after it.

1 + 2

3

docs.title: Values and their types
docs.text:
Every value has a type: 1 + 2 is an Int, "Hello" a String. hql check writes a program's type without evaluating it:

$ hql check - <<< '7 / 2'
Int

Chapter 2 meets the types one by one.

docs.title: Checked before it runs
docs.text:
A program is checked as a whole before anything is evaluated. A type error names the expression it found and points at it:

1 + "two"

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | 1 + "two"
  |     ^^^^^

Nothing ran: there is no value, only the report, and the exit status is 1. The same holds for a name nobody bound:

pages + 1

check error[unknown-name]: `pages` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | pages + 1
  | ^^^^^

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text:
name = expression binds a value to a name for the statements after it. The program's value is its last expression.

pages = 280
chapters = 24
pages / chapters

11

A binding may state its type, and the checker holds the value to it:

rating : Int = 5
rating

5

docs.title: Choosing a value
docs.text:
a given condition otherwise b is a when the condition holds, and b otherwise. It is an expression, so it has a type: both branches have one.

pages = 412
"long" given pages > 300 otherwise "short"

"long"

match compares one value against patterns, in order, and the first that fits gives the result:

status = "reading"
match status {
    "done" => "finished",
    "reading" => "on the nightstand",
    _ => "on the shelf",
}

"on the nightstand"

The checker rejects a match that does not cover every case before it runs; _ is the pattern that fits anything.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 2 meets the data types: Int, Float, String and Bool, tried in the REPL, and Data, the records and lists that JSON and YAML are made of.

docs.title: 3. Collections
docs.text: A Data list holds trees. Most collections in HQL hold values of one known type, and say what they promise about order and repetition. This chapter meets them, and the steps every collection shares.

docs.title: Lists, sets and maps
docs.text:
A list keeps every element at its position, duplicates included:

[412, 280, 310, 145]

[412, 280, 310, 145]

A set keeps each distinct value once and promises no order. Braces around values, rather than fields, write one:

{"novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"}

{"novel", "essay", "poetry"}

A value prints as the literal that writes it, so a set prints in braces and a string inside a collection keeps its quotes. hql check writes a program's type without running it:

{"novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"}

Set<String>

A map pairs each key with one value. Map(keys, values) builds one, and get looks a key up — an Option, since the key may be missing:

pages = Map(["Dune", "Frankenstein"], [412, 280])
get(pages, "Dune")

412

docs.title: A step keeps its input's shape
docs.text:
Steps work on any collection, and each returns the kind of collection it was given wherever it can: a list stays a list, a set stays a set.

[412, 280, 310, 145] | sort | take(2)

[145, 280]

[412, 280, 310, 145] | drop(1)

[280, 310, 145]

A set has no order of its own, so sort gives it one and the result is a list. And because a set keeps each value once, mapping it can make it smaller:

{3, 1, 2} | map(n => n * 0)

{0}

[3, 1, 2] | map(n => n * 0)

[0, 0, 0]

size, count and contains ask about a whole collection:

genres = ["novel", "essay", "novel"]
[genres | size, genres | count("novel")]

[3, 2]

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
sort orders by a value's own order. sort(by = key) orders by a key, and a function of two values that returns an Ordering orders by comparison:

[412, 280, 310] | sort((a, b) => compare(b, a))

[412, 310, 280]

min and max find the least and greatest value. Over an empty list there is none, and the type says so: the result is an Option.

[412, 280, 310] | min

280

[] | List<Int> | min

none

[] | List<Int> is a constructor written as a step: x | T is T(x). A constructor builds a value of its type — Set(xs), List(xs), Map(keys, values) — and the pipeline form reads left to right:

["novel", "essay", "novel", "poetry"] | Set | size

3

docs.title: Positions are promises
docs.text:
A list, a ranking and a sequence of cards have positions; a set does not. The checker rejects a set given to a step that needs positions, and says what to write instead:

{3, 1, 2} | drop(1)

check error[type-mismatch]: `drop` needs values in a stable order, and Set<Int> has none; sort it first
 --> <expression>:1:13
  |
1 | {3, 1, 2} | drop(1)
  |             ^^^^^^^

The checker knows each collection's promises from its type, so this is found before anything runs, not after a wrong answer.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Steps take functions — n => n * 0, (a, b) => compare(b, a). Chapter 4 is about functions themselves: naming them, passing them, and making them generic.

docs.title: 6. SQL-like Queries
docs.text: SQL asks a table questions: which rows, in what order, how many, grouped by what. HQL asks the same questions with pipeline steps. This chapter works through them over one table — the reading club's shelf, written as a list of records.

docs.title: The table
docs.text:
shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", author: "Mary Shelley", year: 1818, genre: "novel", pages: 280, status: "done", rating: 5},
    {title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, genre: "novel", pages: 412, status: "reading"},
    {title: "The Hobbit", author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", year: 1937, genre: "novel", pages: 310, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", author: "Walt Whitman", year: 1855, genre: "poetry", pages: 145, status: "todo"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1929, genre: "essay", pages: 112, status: "done", rating: 4},
    {title: "The Common Reader", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "essay", pages: 304, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "novel", pages: 194, status: "reading"},
]
shelf | size

7

Every program in this chapter begins with these lines; the book shows them once.

docs.title: Select and where
docs.text:
map is SQL's SELECT: it says what to keep of each row. filter is WHERE:

shelf
| filter(b => b.status == "todo")
| map(b => b.title)

["The Hobbit", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]

shelf
| filter(b => b.author == "Virginia Woolf")
| map(b => {title: b.title, year: b.year})

[{title: "A Room of One's Own", year: 1929}, {title: "The Common Reader", year: 1925}, {title: "Mrs Dalloway", year: 1925}]

docs.title: Typed views of a record
docs.text:
ORDER BY pages needs pages to be numbers, and a record's leaves have no type of their own. A small function gives a record a typed view — one field, as the type the program means it to be, with what to do when it is missing:

fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }
fn pages(b: Data) : Int = match b.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }
fn year(b: Data) : Int = match b.year { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

From here on, the programs begin with the table and these views.

docs.title: Order by and limit
docs.text:
sort(by = key) is ORDER BY, and take(n) is LIMIT. A comparison orders the other way:

shelf
| sort(by = year)
| take(3)
| map(title)

["Frankenstein", "Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader"]

shelf
| sort((a, b) => compare(pages(b), pages(a)))
| take(2)
| map(b => {title: title(b), pages: pages(b)})

[{pages: 412, title: "Dune"}, {pages: 310, title: "The Hobbit"}]

docs.title: Distinct
docs.text:
A set keeps each value once, so SELECT DISTINCT is the Set constructor:

shelf | map(b => b.genre) | Set

{"novel", "poetry", "essay"}

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
size counts rows. sum, average, min and max work over numbers, so the pages are read through their view first:

lengths = shelf | map(pages)
{books: lengths | size, pages: lengths | sum, longest: lengths | max, average: lengths | average}

{average: 251.0, books: 7, longest: 412, pages: 1757}

Every aggregate is a fold: reduce with a starting value and a way to combine two values. sum is reduce(0, +). max is reduce(max), which starts from the first value and so is an Option: an empty list has none.

lengths = shelf | map(pages)
{total: lengths | reduce(0, +), longest: lengths | reduce(max)}

{longest: 412, total: 1757}

docs.title: Group by
docs.text:
group(by = key) partitions the rows by a key. Each group holds its key and its items, and a map over the groups computes one row per group — SQL's GROUP BY with its aggregates:

shelf
| group(by = b => b.genre)
| map(g => {genre: g.key, books: g.items | size, pages: g.items | map(pages) | sum})

{{books: 4, genre: "novel", pages: 1196}, {books: 1, genre: "poetry", pages: 145}, {books: 2, genre: "essay", pages: 416}}

HAVING is a filter after the group:

shelf
| group(by = b => b.author)
| filter(g => size(g.items) > 1)
| map(g => g.key)

{"Virginia Woolf"}

docs.title: Several answers in one pass
docs.text:
tee names a side branch of a pipeline. The branch reads the same rows, its result is bound to a name, and the main pipeline goes on unchanged. A branch of several steps continues on lines indented past the | before tee:

reading = shelf
| tee unread =
    filter(b => b.status == "todo")
    | size
| tee read =
    filter(b => b.status == "done")
    | size
| filter(b => b.status == "reading")
| map(title)
{unread: unread, read: read, reading: reading}

{read: 2, reading: ["Dune", "Mrs Dalloway"], unread: 3}

docs.title: From SQL to HQL
docs.text: SQL HQL SELECT title map(b => b.title) WHERE status = 'todo' filter(b => b.status == "todo") ORDER BY year sort(by = year) LIMIT 3 take(3) OFFSET 3 drop(3) SELECT DISTINCT genre map(b => b.genre) \| Set COUNT(*), SUM(pages) size, map(pages) \| sum GROUP BY genre group(by = b => b.genre) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filter(g => size(g.items) > 1)

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: The shelf was written by hand. In chapter 16 the same books are documents in a vault, and the same questions are asked of the documents themselves.

docs.title: 7. Streams that do not end
docs.text: Every collection so far had an end: a size, a last element. A stream is a succession of values whose production need not end — a log, a feed, the natural numbers. HQL types the difference, so a program cannot ask an endless stream a question that needs its end.

docs.title: A function that yields
docs.text:
A fn whose body is a block, in braces, produces its values with yield, in the order each yield is reached. Its result type says whether production ends: Seq<T> promises an end, Stream<T> does not. These are the natural numbers:

fn naturals(from: Int) : Stream<Int> {
    yield from
    for n in naturals(from + 1) {
        yield n
    }
}
naturals(1) | take(5)

[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

for name in collection { … } runs its block once per value. A block that yields is an iterating block: it holds yield, for and bindings, one per line (function bodies).

Calling naturals(1) evaluates nothing. Its value is a recipe for the numbers, and take(5) asks for five of them and then stops asking — which is what makes an endless producer usable.

docs.title: One value at a time
docs.text:
map, filter and drop take a stream and give a stream. Each value passes through the whole pipeline before the next is produced, so only as many are made as the end of the pipeline asks for:

naturals(1)
| filter(n => n % 7 == 0)
| map(n => n * n)
| take(3)

[49, 196, 441]

docs.title: Questions that need the end
docs.text:
sum, size, sort, group and the other whole-input steps need the last value before they can answer. Over a stream there may be none, and the checker says so before anything runs:

fn naturals(from: Int) : Stream<Int> {
    yield from
    for n in naturals(from + 1) {
        yield n
    }
}
naturals(1) | sum

check error[type-mismatch]: `sum` needs a finite input, and Stream<Int> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
 --> <expression>:7:15
  |
7 | naturals(1) | sum
  |               ^^^

A stream becomes finite through take(n), or is answered in pieces through collect(n), which gathers consecutive values into batches of n:

naturals(1)
| collect(3)
| map(batch => batch | sum)
| take(3)

[6, 15, 24]

emit is the inverse of collect: it passes on every member of every batch, in order. flat_map(f) is map(f) | emit.

[[1, 2], [3]] | emit

[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: A sequence over the shelf
docs.text:
A generator that promises an end is a Seq. This one yields the title of each book on the shelf of chapter 6, in title order — a sequence the shelf produces on demand:

shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", pages: 280},
    {title: "Dune", pages: 412},
    {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", pages: 145},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", pages: 112},
    {title: "The Common Reader", pages: 304},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", pages: 194},
]
fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }

fn titles() : Seq<String> {
    for b in shelf | sort(by = title) {
        yield title(b)
    }
}
titles() | take(3)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein"]

A list is such a sequence already. So are the documents of a file read with source, in chapter 9, produced as each one is read.

docs.title: Writing a stream
docs.text:
Formatting an endless stream writes it piece by piece as it arrives: a line of text, a JSON value per line, a CSV row. hql flushes each piece, and a reader that stops reading ends the stream:

naturals(1) | map(n => n * n) | json

$ hql eval '…naturals… | map(n => n * n) | json' | head -3
1
4
9

A diagram format describes a whole, so | mermaid over a stream is a type error until take(n) bounds it.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 8 is about every format a value can be written in, and who chooses it.

docs.title: 8. Writing results out
docs.text:
A program's value is computed first, and written second. How it is written is a presentation format — plain text, HQL, Markdown, JSON, YAML, CSV, or a diagram — and the format is a type, so a program that formats a value knows what kind of text it holds.

The programs of this chapter read the shelf of chapter 6, with its typed views, and the book shows these lines once:

shelf = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", author: "Mary Shelley", year: 1818, genre: "novel", pages: 280, status: "done"},
    {title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, genre: "novel", pages: 412, status: "reading"},
    {title: "The Hobbit", author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", year: 1937, genre: "novel", pages: 310, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Leaves of Grass", author: "Walt Whitman", year: 1855, genre: "poetry", pages: 145, status: "todo"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1929, genre: "essay", pages: 112, status: "done"},
    {title: "The Common Reader", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "essay", pages: 304, status: "todo"},
    {title: "Mrs Dalloway", author: "Virginia Woolf", year: 1925, genre: "novel", pages: 194, status: "reading"},
]
fn title(b: Data) : String = match b.title { some(String t) => t, _ => "" }
fn pages(b: Data) : Int = match b.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

docs.title: Formats are a category of their own
docs.text:
Each format is a Format: Text, Lines, Hql, Markdown, Hmd, Json, JsonLines, Yaml, Csv, D2 and Mermaid. A format describes how values are written, not the text itself: a step named for a format encodes any value in it, and what comes out is a String:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title) | markdown

- The Hobbit
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title) | markdown

String

A formatted value is a string that remembers its format, so a host prints it as it is. A later step may read it, and comparing it with a string compares the text:

([1, 2] | json) == "[\n  1,\n  2\n]"

true

docs.title: The longhand, format
docs.text:
markdown is the shorthand for format(Markdown). The longhand takes two options. limit keeps the first n elements and says how many were cut:

shelf
| map(title)
| format(Text, limit = 3)

["Frankenstein", "Dune", "The Hobbit"]
… 4 more not shown

A list of records in Markdown is a bullet list. A table is a value of its own type, Table: Table(xs, columns = [...]) takes one row per record and the columns in the order written, and every format writes it as a table, a pipe table in Markdown:

shelf
| map(b => {title: title(b), pages: pages(b)})
| Table(columns = ["title", "pages"])
| markdown

| title               | pages |
| ------------------- | ----- |
| Frankenstein        | 280   |
| Dune                | 412   |
| The Hobbit          | 310   |
| Leaves of Grass     | 145   |
| A Room of One's Own | 112   |
| The Common Reader   | 304   |
| Mrs Dalloway        | 194   |

The same table in Csv is a header row and one row per record, in Json an array of objects with their keys in column order, and in Text space-aligned columns. renderer names one of a format's encoders for a shape over the project's choice, format(Markdown, renderer = "mermaid") for a graph; a table renderer, such as pipe, writes only a Table.

A format that cannot write a value is a type error, reported before the program runs:

1 | d2

check error[type-mismatch]: no renderer writes Int as D2
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | 1 | d2
  |     ^^

docs.title: Choosing the format from outside
docs.text:
A program that does not format its result is written as HQL — the literal you would type to get the value back, a string in quotes. --to text writes a string bare instead, and --to names any other format without changing the program:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | map(title)

- The Hobbit
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader

--to none evaluates the program and writes nothing. --envelope json wraps the answer for another program to read: the type, the value, and every diagnostic the run wrote:

shelf | filter(b => b.status == "todo") | size

{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "origin": "<expression>",
  "type": "Int",
  "value": 3
}

The order is fixed: a format step in the program wins, then --to, then the host's own — Markdown for a document, HQL for a terminal.

docs.title: A project chooses its renderers
docs.text:
Which renderer writes a type in a format is a project's choice, in the hql.toml of the vault a program runs in (chapter 16), over the built-in defaults. A graph in Markdown is a D2 diagram unless the file says otherwise:

[format.Graph]
markdown = "mermaid"

A renderer or format the binary does not have fails loading the vault, so the mistake is reported before any query runs.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every value so far was written to the terminal. Chapter 9 reads files, standard input and the network, and writes files and standard output, without leaving the language.

docs.title: 13. Working with hql
docs.text: The language is half of what you use; the other half is the command and what it says back. This chapter is about the tools: the commands, the diagnostics, and the messages hql writes when a program is wrong.

docs.title: The commands
docs.text:
Command What it does hql eval <program> check and evaluate a program given as an argument hql run <file> check and evaluate a program in a file; - reads standard input hql check <file> write the program's type, and the signature of every alias, without evaluating hql repl read, evaluate and print, keeping bindings between lines hql render <file> build a document from its cells (chapter 19) hql builtins list every step, by the provider that implements it, with its signature hql config the settings in force, and where each came from hql doctor check the semantic-search chain and name the first missing part

--vault <dir> names the vault, --to <format> the output format, and --envelope json wraps the answer for another program.

docs.title: The REPL
docs.text:
hql repl keeps its bindings from one input to the next. The arrow keys edit a line and recall earlier inputs, from a history kept between sessions. An input goes on over several lines while a bracket is open, or while the next line opens with |, so every program in this book can be pasted in as it is written. :type asks for the type of an expression, or, given a function's name, prints the standard library's declarations of it, one per overload. :quit leaves, as do quit, exit and Ctrl-D:

$ hql repl
hql 0.5.1. `:help` for commands, `:quit` to leave.
hql> shelf = [412, 280]
()
hql> shelf | sum
692
hql> :type shelf
List<Int>
hql> :type range
fn range(start: Int, end: Int, step: Int = 1) : List<Int>    // std/seq
hql> :quit

docs.title: What a step takes
docs.text:
hql builtins lists every step with its signature, one line per form:

$ hql builtins
core 0.5.0 (always available)
  size
    Collection<T> | size<T>() -> Int
    Count all element occurrences.
  contains
    Collection<T> | contains<T>(value: T (positional)) -> Bool
    Whether a value occurs in the collection.
  …

A function of a module that the program has not imported is listed too, so the import it needs can be looked up. import lexical makes a module visible; lexical.lexical(…) names a function with its module, when two visible modules declare one name and the input does not tell them apart. The modules of lib/std/prelude.hql, string, seq, math, option, result, graph, format and io among them, are visible in every program unless the vault's hql.toml says prelude = false.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
A run produces a value and the diagnostics its phases wrote: warnings that change nothing, errors that make a result wrong, failures that make one impossible. Each is headed by the phase that wrote it, its severity and its kind, and names where it points, by line and column. Chapter 12 is the whole error model.

By default hql stops at the first error. --report collect reports every error it can find:

$ hql --report collect eval 'a = nosuchthing
b = alsomissing'
check error[unknown-name]: `nosuchthing` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | a = nosuchthing
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^

check error[unknown-name]: `alsomissing` is not bound
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 | b = alsomissing
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^

2 diagnostics: 0 failure, 2 error, 0 warning

A misspelled step suggests the nearest one, and a retired name says what replaced it, on a help line under the caret:

$ hql eval '[1, 2] | mapp(n => n)'
check error[unknown-step]: `mapp` is not a pipeline step
 --> <expression>:1:10
  |
1 | [1, 2] | mapp(n => n)
  |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: did you mean `map`?

A warning never changes the exit status. Names have one casing per kind — snake_case for bindings, functions and fields, PascalCase for types — and a name off its kind's convention is a warning where it is written:

$ hql eval 'bookCount = 7
bookCount'
7
check warning[naming-convention]: `bookCount` is a binding, written in snake_case
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | bookCount = 7
  | ^^^^^^^^^
  = help: write it `book_count`

--envelope json carries every diagnostic, whatever the level, as data, and --diagnostics-format json writes each one to standard error as one JSON document per line. A program that wants to report on itself, apart from its result, writes to a logger: the logging page of chapter 9.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The report mode and level come from the command line, then the vault's hql.toml, then the environment ($HQL_REPORT, $HQL_REPORT_LEVEL), then the defaults. hql config says which applies, and why:

$ hql config
report mode: strict (from the default)
report level: warning (from the default)
backend: localhost (from the default)
vault: none

backend is the execution backend of chapter 14, and localhost is the only one. Run inside a vault, or with --vault, the last line names it and counts its cards.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every chapter so far was about a step. Chapter 14 is about the pipeline the steps form: what | does, when a program is checked, where it runs, and the systems a pipeline will connect.

docs.title: 14. Pipelines
docs.text: Part I was about the steps: what each one takes, what it gives, and the type that joins them. This part is about the pipeline the steps form, and the systems a pipeline connects. This chapter is the frame; chapter 15 is the story it frames, an ETL pipeline written as one file.

docs.title: A pipeline language
docs.text:
An HQL program is values flowing through typed steps. | is the operator that forms a step: the value on its left becomes the input of the operation on its right, and the result is the input of the next. A step invokes exactly one operation, filter, sort, map, or one presentation, json, markdown:

[3, 1, 2] | filter(n => n > 1) | sort | map(n => n * 10)

[20, 30]

A dot is not a step. s.trim() is a receiver call, and b.title a field read; both are expression evaluation inside the step that holds them, and neither is a position in the pipeline:

["Dune ", " Emma"] | map(s => s.trim().upper())

["DUNE", "EMMA"]

The two operators answer two questions. | says what happens to the whole collection, one operation at a time, in the order written. . says what is computed from one value, inside one of those operations. A reader finds the shape of a program in its pipes, and the detail of each stage in its dots.

docs.title: Three phases
docs.text:
A program is parsed, then checked, then executed, and a diagnostic is headed by the phase that wrote it: parse failure and check error before anything runs, execute failure after (chapter 12). Checking resolves every name, import and module, infers and checks every type, and verifies every trait implementation; a program the checker rejects has no meaning, and no step of it executes. hql check runs the first two phases alone and prints the type the third would produce:

[3, 1, 2] | filter(n => n > 1) | sort | map(n => n * 10)

List<Int>

Execution is a strategy a backend chooses. localhost, the one backend the current release has, evaluates the checked program step by step, each step run to completion before the next, in memory. A backend that compiles a program, or runs it over many machines, is bound to the same contract: it accepts exactly what the checker accepts, and it computes the value localhost computes, at the same type, with the same failure where localhost fails. There is no syntax for choosing a backend, because a program's answer does not depend on it; the choice is configuration, and hql config reports it.

docs.title: The unit of execution
docs.text:
A step is the unit of execution. It runs over its whole input, and a backend may not break it, reorder it against an effect, or run it twice. Two rules follow.

An effectful step, one that reaches outside the program, source, target, sink, a logger's info, runs once, where it is written, in program order. A backend may plan how the pure steps between two effects are fused or distributed; it may not move an effect, and a backend that cannot run a program refuses it before running any part of it.

A pure step may be rewritten by its shape. A step that decides each value alone, filter, map, may run over any part of the input in any order; a step that needs the whole input, sort, group, sum, size, is where the parts meet, and the pipeline holds nothing in between. The reading list of chapter 16 is three such steps: filter decides each card on its own, sort needs every card before it can place the first, and map turns each card into its title. That alternation of per-value steps and whole-input steps is the shape of MapReduce, and HQL keeps it visible in the pipeline: nothing is stored between steps, and nothing is a loop. collect(n) and emit change the shape of what flows, batches of values or their members, and tee branches a pipeline without ending it; each of them is a step like any other, and the type says what the next step may ask.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text: The smallest pipeline is a shell pipe. hql '<program>' reads standard input with source(stdin, Json), writes its result as jq or awk would, and names no input or output of its own: input is source or tap in the program, output is target or sink in the program, or the result, presented by --to. The command-line page of chapter 9 shows each flag; one program there reads a log as it is written, appends its errors to a file and prints every message, with no orchestration around it. The query is the dataflow, and the shell is the simplest backend of all.

docs.title: Connecting systems
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before they ship.

The systems a data platform joins, queues, databases, services, scheduled jobs, are endpoints and configured sources to a pipeline. Each is reached by source, tap, target and sink, with the type saying whether it ends.

Configured sources keep connection details out of programs. A program names an id; hql.toml names the system, and a secret is read from the environment the configuration names, never written in either:

[sources.sightings]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "BIRDS_DSN"
table = "sightings"

type Sighting { species : String, site : String, seen : String }

sightings : Seq<Sighting> = source("sightings")
sightings | group(by = s => s.species) | map(g => {species: g.key, seen: g.items | size})

A relational table is a Seq of rows read through the schema boundary of chapter 9; a write by id is target("sightings"), in the mode the configuration states. A connection string in a program is a type error today, and stays one.

Messaging systems such as Kafka and NATS are live endpoints. A topic is read by tap, as a Stream, and written by sink, one document per value; collect(n) batches what is written, and partition(by = key) states which values belong together, a logical unit a backend may map onto the system's own partitions without the program naming them:

[sources.events]
kind = "kafka"
brokers_env = "KAFKA_BROKERS"
topic = "sightings"

tap("events")
| filter(e => e.seen == "night")
| partition(by = e => e.site)
| sink("alerts")

Network endpoints, http, websocket and socket under import net, are in the current release, on the network page. An HTTP resource read once is a Seq; a socket is a Stream.

A pipeline file is a job. What a data platform calls a job, a notebook or a workflow, sources, transformations, sinks and a schedule, is an .hql file whose steps are the transformations and whose source and sink steps are its edges; the schedule, the credentials and the backend are configuration around it, and hql check reads the configuration and opens nothing. The same file runs on localhost from a terminal and, as design direction, on a backend that distributes its pure steps, with the same answer.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 15 puts the frame to work: a pipeline that reads a queue, enriches what it reads from a database, and writes tables, alerts and an archive, in one checked file.

docs.title: 15. ETL pipelines
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: apart from the diagnostics the current binary already gives, these programs do not run, and names, kinds, types and outputs may change before any of it ships. It is a story about where the pipeline of chapter 14 is going, told in one file.

Every data platform has a language for the wiring. Data Factory wires activities in JSON, PySpark in a DataFrame API, ksqlDB in SQL over topics, Kafka Streams in Java, dbt in SQL models with a dependency graph around them. Each describes the same four things: where data comes from, what is done to it, where it goes, and when. They differ in where a mistake is found: in a validator before deployment, in a cluster at run time, or in a dashboard the next morning.

HQL's claim is that the wiring is a program like any other in this book. A pipeline is one .hql file; its sources and targets are ids that configuration binds to systems; its types are checked before anything connects; and the same text runs over a queue that never ends and over the archive of what the queue once carried.

docs.title: A pipeline is a file
docs.text:
A field station publishes bird sightings from its sensors to a Kafka topic. A Postgres database holds the sites and receives daily counts. Alerts go to a second topic, and everything read is archived as JSON Lines. The station's hql.toml names each of those systems once:

[sources.sightings]
kind = "kafka"
brokers_env = "KAFKA_BROKERS"
topic = "sightings"
group = "station-nightly"

[sources.sites]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "STATION_DSN"
table = "sites"

[sources.daily_counts]
kind = "postgres"
dsn_env = "STATION_DSN"
table = "daily_counts"
mode = "append"

[sources.alerts]
kind = "kafka"
brokers_env = "KAFKA_BROKERS"
topic = "alerts"

[sources.archive]
kind = "json_lines"
path = "archive/sightings.jsonl"
mode = "append"

The pipeline, nightly.hql, names only the ids:

type Sighting { species : String, site : String, seen : String, at : DateTime }
type Site     { site : String, region : String, protected : Bool }
type Count    { day : Date, region : String, species : String, sightings : Int }

sites : Seq<Site> = source("sites")

tap("sightings")
| Sighting
| tee archived = sink("archive")
| join(sites, on = (s, p) => s.site == p.site)
| map(j => {species: j.left.species, region: j.right.region, protected: j.right.protected, at: j.left.at})
| tee alerts =
    filter(x => x.protected and x.species == "barn owl")
    | map(x => {region: x.region, at: x.at, text: fmt("barn owl in protected {}", x.region)})
    | sink("alerts")
| window(1d, by = x => x.at)
| map(w => w
    | group(by = x => {region: x.region, species: x.species})
    | map(g => Count(day = w.start.date, region = g.key.region, species = g.key.species, sightings = g.items | size)))
| emit
| sink("daily_counts")

Read top to bottom, it is the dataflow diagram a platform would draw: one input, a lookup, two side outputs, a windowed aggregate, one main output. There is no orchestration around it, no activity names, no cluster configuration in the text. hql check nightly.hql reads hql.toml, resolves every id to its kind and every kind to a type, checks the whole file, and opens no connection.

docs.title: Ids, not connections
docs.text:
source("sites") and tap("sightings") name configuration. The id is a literal, because the type of what it reads is known only from the configuration, and a program whose source could be computed would have a type nobody could check. Three refusals exist today, on the sources-by-id page of chapter 9: a computed id and a connection string in place of an id are check errors, the second saying where connection details belong, and an id the configuration does not declare is a check error naming the nearest one.

A binding can break, and the design is that it breaks at the earliest phase that can see it. Checking sees configuration; evaluation sees the system:

What is wrong When it is found What is said source("sightngs") checking check error[unknown-name]: no source sightngs is configured; did you mean sightings? sites : Seq<Site> = source("sightings") checking check error[type-mismatch]: sightings is a kafka source, read by tap as a Stream, not by source as a Seq source("sites") read as Seq<Count> checking check error[type-mismatch]: the boundary of sites has no field day; Count declares one STATION_DSN not set evaluation, before the first row execute failure[io-failure]: source sites reads its connection from $STATION_DSN, which is not set a row whose protected is "yes" evaluation, at that row execute failure[io-failure]: source sites: row 14 does not decode as Site: field protected: "yes" is not a Bool the broker unreachable evaluation, before the first message execute failure[io-failure]: source sightings: no broker at $KAFKA_BROKERS answered

A secret is named by the environment variable that holds it and never printed. A failure at evaluation names the source by its id, the system by its configured name, and the row or message by its position, as a CSV decode error does today; what it never does is continue past a row it could not read and count it later as missing.

The configuration is also where a system's names meet the program's. The sites table may call its region column region_code; the boundary of chapter 9 maps it, [sources.sites.fields.region] name = "region_code", and the program keeps the name it reads. Renaming a column is a change to one line of configuration, not to every pipeline that reads it.

docs.title: Streams in, tables out
docs.text:
tap("sightings") is a Stream<Data>, and | Sighting reads each message as a declared record, so the rest of the file is typed. source("sites") is a Seq<Site>: a table is finite, read once, replayable within the evaluation. The join between them is the common shape of enrichment, a stream against a lookup, and the type says why it is cheap: the finite side is read whole, the live side passes through one message at a time, and no message waits for another.

Two streams joined would wait for each other without end, and the checker says so: join over two Streams is refused until one of them is bounded by a window. A window is collect by time rather than by count, window(1d, by = x => x.at), a Stream<Seq<T>> whose batches close when the day does. Inside a batch every whole-input step of chapter 6 applies, which is how the daily counts are a group and a size over an endless input. emit lets the counts out one at a time, and sink("daily_counts") appends each as a row.

The two tee branches write without ending the pipeline. The archive is every sighting as it arrived, before enrichment; the alerts are a filter and a map, written to a topic as messages. A tee branch is the fan-out a platform draws as a diamond, and it is typed like everything else: a branch that ended in target over the stream would be refused, because a stream may never complete, and sink is what a stream is written with.

docs.title: From a batch to a stream, and back
docs.text:
A pipeline written for a live topic is a pipeline written for its history, because the steps are the same and the type is the only difference. The archive is a file, so source("archive") is a Seq<Data>; stream turns a finite sequence into a stream that produces its elements in order and then ends, so the nightly pipeline replays a day from the archive with the topic replaced and nothing else changed:

fn nightly(sightings: Stream<Sighting>) : Unit = …

source("archive") | Sighting | filter(s => s.at.date == Date(2026, 10, 24)) | stream | nightly

The other direction is as short. A stream becomes one file by bounding it and writing the bound: take(n) for a count, window for a span, collect(n) for batches of a size:

tap("sightings") | window(1h) | emit | sink(file("last-hour.jsonl"), Json)

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | take(2) | target(file("two.json"))

A backfill is the first program over the archive; a snapshot is the second over the topic; a replay for a test is either over a file of recorded messages, with no broker at all. The platform words, backfill, snapshot, replay, name three ways to bound or unbound one pipeline, not three pipelines.

docs.title: Rows that do not decode
docs.text:
A pipeline over a queue meets messages that are not what the type says. The default is the strict one above: the first such message stops the evaluation, naming it. A pipeline that must keep running routes them instead. Sighting? reads each message as a Result<Sighting, Invalid>, and fork splits a stream of results into its two sides without ending either:

tap("sightings")
| Sighting?
| fork
| tee rejected =
    errs()
    | map(e => {message: e.input, why: e.violations | map(v => v.message)})
    | sink("dead_letter")
| oks()
| nightly

The dead-letter queue is a sink like the others, and what reaches it is a value: the message as it arrived and every violation at once, the way validation as a value reports them. Nothing is logged and lost; the rejected rows are a source another pipeline reads.

docs.title: Partitions, schedules and backends
docs.text:
Three things a platform configures stay out of the file.

A partition is the logical unit of ownership: partition(by = x => x.region) states that values of one region belong together, so a windowed group per region may run wherever that region's values are. It names no worker and no Kafka partition; a backend maps the logical partitions onto its own, and the local backend runs them one after another with the same result.

A schedule is configuration beside the sources, [jobs.nightly] run = "nightly.hql" with an at, or a trigger that is itself a source, a topic whose messages start a run. The file does not know when it runs.

A backend is the execution strategy of chapter 14: localhost in a terminal, a distributed one in a cluster, chosen by [execution] backend or --backend, and bound to compute what localhost computes. hql check is the same under every backend, and it is what a deployment runs before it deploys: the configuration, the types and the file, with no system touched.

docs.title: What each of them wires
docs.text:
Sources and sinks Transformations Where a mistake is found Data Factory linked services and datasets, in JSON activities, each a box at validation of the JSON, or in the run's monitor PySpark readers and writers, in code DataFrame operations when the job runs, at the operation that fails ksqlDB topics as streams and tables SQL over them when the statement is submitted, or in the records it skips dbt models over a warehouse SQL, with tests after when the model builds, or when its tests run HQL, as designed ids bound in hql.toml the steps of this book when the file is checked, before anything connects

The columns are the same four things. What HQL adds is a type for each arrow, so that stream against table, finite against live, declared record against configured boundary, are checked where the file is written, and the file that passed is the file that runs.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Part III reads a different kind of data. Chapter 16 opens a folder of documents and asks it the questions chapter 6 asked a table.

docs.title: 16. A vault of documents
docs.text: The shelf of chapter 6 was a list written by hand. Here the same books are documents in a folder, and HQL reads the folder. This part of the book is about knowledge: documents, the links between them, their meaning, and the agents that read them.

docs.title: A vault is a folder
docs.text:
A vault is a directory of Markdown and HyperMarkDown documents. The tutorial vault looks like this:

examples/tutorial/
├── authors/
│   ├── frank-herbert.hmd
│   ├── jrr-tolkien.hmd
│   ├── mary-shelley.hmd
│   ├── virginia-woolf.hmd
│   └── walt-whitman.hmd
├── books/
│   ├── a-room-of-ones-own.hmd
│   ├── dune.hmd
│   ├── frankenstein.hmd
│   ├── leaves-of-grass.hmd
│   ├── mrs-dalloway.hmd
│   ├── the-common-reader.hmd
│   └── the-hobbit.hmd
├── club.hmd
├── frankenstein-inspires-dune.hmd
├── librarian.hmd
└── hql.toml

Each document is a card. A card has a header of metadata and a body someone wrote:

---
title: Dune
metadata:
  category: book
  author: Frank Herbert
  year: 1965
  genre: novel
  pages: 412
  status: reading
---
# Dune

A novel by [[frank-herbert]]. A desert planet, a spice, and a family that inherits both.

A program run inside a vault runs against it: hql takes the nearest directory at or above the current one that holds .hmd/ or hql.toml. --vault <directory> names one instead:

hql --vault examples/tutorial eval 'cards | size'

cards | size

15

docs.title: cards
docs.text:
cards is every card of the vault, as a sequence. Its order is the order a sorted walk of the folder reaches each document — the entries of each directory by name, depth first — so a program answers the same on every machine:

cards | take(4) | map(c => c.name)

["frank-herbert", "jrr-tolkien", "mary-shelley", "virginia-woolf"]

A card has the fields of a document: its name (the file stem), title, path, format, body, its kind, and metadata, the header's tree.

docs.title: A link is an optional card
docs.text:
@[[name]] refers to a card by name: @ followed by the link a document writes, [[name]]. A link may point at a document nobody has written yet, so its type is Option<Card>, and reading a field through it reads through the option:

@[[dune]].title

"Dune"

@[[nowhere]].title

none

docs.title: Metadata is Data
docs.text:
A card's metadata is the Data of chapter 2, so every question from chapters 2 and 6 applies. The books are the cards whose category says so:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(c => c.title)

["A Room of One's Own", "Dune", "Frankenstein", "Leaves of Grass", "Mrs Dalloway", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"]

docs.title: The reading list
docs.text:
The club's reading list is the books still to read, by title:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)

["Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"]

Read it as three steps, each consuming the one before: filter decides each card on its own, sort needs every card before it can place the first, and map turns each card into its title. Nothing is stored in between, and nothing is a loop.

No one maintains this list. Mark a book status: done in its header and the next run of the query no longer lists it.

docs.title: Writing cards
docs.text:
The formats of chapter 8 apply to a card as to any value. A card written as Markdown is its body; a list of cards, a list of links:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "author") | markdown

- [[frank-herbert]]
- [[jrr-tolkien]]
- [[mary-shelley]]
- [[virginia-woolf]]
- [[walt-whitman]]

docs.title: Grouping cards
docs.text:
group partitions the books by a header value, as it partitioned the shelf:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.status)
| map(g => {status: g.key, books: g.items | map(c => c.title)})

{{books: ["A Room of One's Own", "Frankenstein"], status: "done"}, {books: ["Dune", "Mrs Dalloway"], status: "reading"}, {books: ["Leaves of Grass", "The Common Reader", "The Hobbit"], status: "todo"}}

A typed view of a card works as the views of chapter 6 did, and the pages per author are a map over each group and a sum — map, then reduce:

fn pages(c: Card) : Int = match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => n, _ => 0 }

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| group(by = c => c.metadata.author)
| map(g => {author: g.key, pages: g.items | map(pages) | sum})

{{author: "Virginia Woolf", pages: 610}, {author: "Frank Herbert", pages: 412}, {author: "Mary Shelley", pages: 280}, {author: "Walt Whitman", pages: 145}, {author: "J. R. R. Tolkien", pages: 310}}

docs.title: Kinds of card
docs.text:
A card whose header declares a relation between two other cards is a RelationCard; every other card is a ConceptCard. of_type keeps the cards of one kind:

cards | of_type(RelationCard) | map(c => c.title)

["Frankenstein inspires Dune"]

Chapter 17 is about what that relation means: cards and the links between them form a graph.

docs.title: The vault itself
docs.text:
cards is a binding the standard library makes, cards = vault.cards, over vault, the value the host seeds when it is given a vault:

[vault.name, vault.cards | size | text]

["tutorial", 15]

Outside every vault and without --vault there is no vault, and naming one says so:

cards | size

check error[unknown-name]: `cards` needs a vault: run inside one or pass --vault <directory>
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | cards | size
  | ^^^^^

docs.title: A vault is a namespace
docs.text:
A card is a file with a place in a vault, and the place is what makes it addressable by name: [[dune]] names a card because there is one tree to resolve the name in. That tree is a namespace, rooted at the vault's directory, and a vault is exactly one namespace. cards holds what a wikilink can reach and nothing else, and a card's path is its place in the vault, relative to the root, so the cards of one folder are a filter on the path:

cards | filter(c => c.path | starts_with("books/")) | size

7

docs.title: Other vaults
docs.text:
A second vault is a second namespace. It is reached as a configured source of kind vault (sources and targets by id), with its own cards and graph, and its cards are never merged into cards: a wikilink in one vault never resolves into another, and a relation between cards of two vaults is a join's result, not a link. The field station of the data sources examples configures two:

journal = source("journal")
archive = source("archive")
[journal.cards | map(c => c.name), archive.cards | map(c => c.name)]

[["kite", "owl", "wren"], ["finch", "heron"]]

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A document that writes [[frank-herbert]] links to another. Chapter 17 follows the links, and the cards and links together are a graph.

docs.title: 17. Links and graphs
docs.text: A document that writes [[frankenstein]] links to another. The links of a vault make its cards a graph: cards are the nodes, links are the edges. This chapter follows links, builds graphs, and draws them.

docs.title: Following links
docs.text:
An edge goes from the card that wrote the link, its source, to the card it names, its target. uplinks gives the edges leaving a card, and downlinks the edges arriving at it:

@[[mrs-dalloway]] | uplinks

[mrs-dalloway -> virginia-woolf]

@[[virginia-woolf]] | downlinks | map(e => e.source)

["a-room-of-ones-own", "mrs-dalloway", "the-common-reader"]

A link in a body may carry data of its own, written after it in braces: [[bearer-tokens]] {relation: defines}. The edge holds it as e.data.

docs.title: Building a graph
docs.text:
Graph(cards) — or cards | Graph — is the graph of those cards and the links among them:

cards
| filter(c => c.name == "virginia-woolf" or c.metadata.author == "Virginia Woolf")
| Graph
| text

a-room-of-ones-own
  -> virginia-woolf
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
the-common-reader
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf
  -> a-room-of-ones-own
  -> mrs-dalloway
  -> the-common-reader

A graph is a value with two fields, both sets: its nodes, the cards, and its edges. The vault's whole graph is bound as graph:

{nodes: graph.nodes | size, edges: graph.edges | size}

{edges: 22, nodes: 14}

A graph can also be built from edges alone, Graph(edges), or from cards and edges together, Graph(nodes, edges). Its nodes are the cards given and every edge's endpoints:

@[[virginia-woolf]] | downlinks | Graph | text

a-room-of-ones-own
  -> virginia-woolf
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
the-common-reader
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf

docs.title: Growing a graph
docs.text:
expand(depth = n) starts from some cards and follows links outwards, n steps, in both directions. Every node it reaches records why it is present — which card it was reached from, and how far away:

@[[mrs-dalloway]] | expand(depth = 1) | text

club  (expanded from mrs-dalloway at depth 1)
  -> mrs-dalloway
mrs-dalloway
  -> virginia-woolf
virginia-woolf  (expanded from mrs-dalloway at depth 1)
  -> mrs-dalloway

direction = "uplinks" or "downlinks" follows links one way only. A graph of matches and their neighbours never claims that the neighbours matched: the reason travels with each node.

docs.title: A relation is an edge
docs.text:
The card frankenstein-inspires-dune declares a relation in its header:

---
title: Frankenstein inspires Dune
metadata:
  category: influence
  knowledge:
    type: Relation
    relation:
      source: frankenstein
      target: dune
---

In a graph such a card is not a node but the edge it declares, between the two cards it names:

cards | of_type(RelationCard) | Graph | text

dune  (expanded from frankenstein-inspires-dune at depth 1)
frankenstein  (expanded from frankenstein-inspires-dune at depth 1)
  -> dune

docs.title: Drawing a graph
docs.text:
A graph is written in a diagram format by the step named for it. mermaid writes a Mermaid diagram and d2 a D2 one; json writes the node-link form a graph library reads:

cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | Graph | mermaid

graph LR
  n0["a-room-of-ones-own"]
  n1["dune"]
  n2["frankenstein"]
  n3["leaves-of-grass"]
  n4["mrs-dalloway"]
  n5["the-common-reader"]
  n6["the-hobbit"]
  n2 --> n1

In a Markdown document — chapter 19 — a graph is written as a fenced d2 block, which documentation sites draw.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: expand grew a graph from a starting card. Chapter 18 finds the starting cards for a question in words.

docs.title: 18. Finding cards by meaning
docs.text: filter answers a question with a yes or no per card. Retrieval answers a question in words with a ranking: every card that matches, best first, each with a score. HQL has two retrievals, each an extension a program imports.

docs.title: Lexical retrieval
docs.text:
lexical matches the words of a query against the words of each card. It needs nothing built in advance:

import lexical
cards | lexical("desert spice") | take(3)

[dune (0.2928), frankenstein-inspires-dune (0.2778), frankenstein (0.2471)]

import lexical makes the extension's step available to the program. Without it, the name is not a step, and the error says which import provides it:

cards | lexical("desert spice")

check error[unknown-name]: `lexical` is provided by the `lexical` extension: write `import lexical`
 --> <expression>:1:9
  |
1 | cards | lexical("desert spice")
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: A ranking holds hits
docs.text:
A ranking is a sequence of hits. A hit holds the card it retrieved, as value, and its score:

import lexical
cards
| lexical("desert spice")
| take(2)
| map(h => {card: h.value.name, score: h.score})

[{card: "dune", score: 0.2927674902397191}, {card: "frankenstein-inspires-dune", score: 0.2777641653663699}]

A score is evidence that a card is relevant to the query, not relevance itself, so every hit carries the retrieval that produced it — the model, the index, the metric, and whether the search was approximate:

import lexical
ranked = cards | lexical("desert")
{model: ranked.retrieval.model, metric: ranked.retrieval.metric, approximate: ranked.retrieval.approximate}

{approximate: false, metric: "cosine", model: "hql.hashbag.v1"}

take keeps a ranking a ranking, in the retrieval's order. Any other order is the program's own: sorting a ranking by another key makes it a plain sequence of hits.

docs.title: Retrieval, then the graph
docs.text:
A ranking is a collection of cards, so every step of the earlier chapters applies. expand grows a graph from the best hits, and the nodes it adds say they were reached, not retrieved:

import lexical
cards
| lexical("a creature and its maker")
| take(2)
| expand(depth = 1)
| text

club  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
  -> dune
  -> frankenstein
  -> leaves-of-grass
dune  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
frankenstein  (retrieved 0.2064)
  -> mary-shelley
  -> dune
leaves-of-grass  (expanded from walt-whitman at depth 1)
  -> walt-whitman
mary-shelley  (expanded from frankenstein at depth 1)
  -> frankenstein
walt-whitman  (retrieved 0.1261)
  -> leaves-of-grass

docs.title: Semantic retrieval
docs.text:
lexical matches spellings: a card that never uses the query's words scores nothing, and a card that uses common ones scores something. semantic scores by meaning, against embeddings a language model computed ahead of time into an index the vault names in hql.toml:

[semantics]
index = ".hql/index.sqlite"

Asked for a creature and its maker, semantic ranks Frankenstein, the relation card that names it, and Mary Shelley, though none of the three contains the word "creature":

import semantic
cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3) | map(h => h.value.title)

["Frankenstein", "Frankenstein inspires Dune", "Mary Shelley"]

The same question, by spelling, finds Frankenstein and then two cards that share only its small words:

import lexical
cards | lexical("a creature and its maker") | take(3) | map(h => h.value.title)

["Frankenstein", "Walt Whitman", "Librarian"]

A semantic ranking reports the model that embedded the cards, so two indexes built by two models are never compared by score:

import semantic
ranked = cards | semantic("a creature and its maker")
{model: ranked.retrieval.model, metric: ranked.retrieval.metric, approximate: ranked.retrieval.approximate}

{approximate: false, metric: "cosine", model: "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"}

The binary never loads a model: contrib/semantics/ embeds the cards and builds the index, and embeds each question the index will be asked, named at build time with --query. The tutorial vault's index holds the three questions this book asks. A question it does not hold is a diagnostic naming the build command, not a ranking of nothing:

import semantic
cards | semantic("night hunting birds") | take(1)

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the index holds no vector for `night hunting birds`, and this binary has no model to make one: rerun `hql-semantics build --query "night hunting birds"`
 --> <expression>:2:9
  |
2 | cards | semantic("night hunting birds") | take(1)
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

hql doctor checks the chain — vault, configuration, index, model, query vectors — and names the first part that is missing.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A ranking, a graph and a reading list are values a program prints. Chapter 19 writes them into the document that asks for them, and builds the document from its queries.

docs.title: 19. Queries inside documents
docs.text: A document can hold the queries that compute parts of it. hql render runs them and builds the document they describe, so a reading list, an index or a status table is a query, not a list somebody keeps up to date.

docs.title: Cells
docs.text:
A fenced block whose info string is hql — or hql#eval, or hql#query — is a cell. This is examples/notebook/reading-list.hmd:

# The club's reading list

Built from the vault with `hql --vault examples/tutorial render`.

```hql id=books hidden
cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
```

## Still to read

```hql id=todo
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```

## How far along

```hql
{books: books | size, to_read: todo | size}
```

docs.title: Building the document
docs.text:
hql render runs every cell against the vault and writes the document with each cell replaced by its output, as Markdown:

hql --vault examples/tutorial render examples/notebook/reading-list.hmd

# The club's reading list

Built from the vault with `hql --vault examples/tutorial render`.

## Still to read

- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit

## How far along

| key     | value |
| ------- | ----- |
| books   | 7     |
| to_read | 3     |

The source is the program; the built document is its result. --write <file> writes the build to a file instead of standard output.

docs.title: Cells share values
docs.text:
A cell's info string carries attributes after its kind:

  • id=<name> exports the cell's value to the other cells of the document, under that name. books and todo above are such names.
  • hidden runs the cell and writes nothing, for a value other cells read.
  • replace or after chooses where that one cell's output goes.

Only a cell's value leaves it: a binding inside a cell stays in that cell. The cells form a dependency graph, and run in the order their reads require, not the order they are written in. A cycle or a duplicate id is an error naming the cells, and a cell that reads a failed one is skipped, saying which cell it waited on.

The document is checked as a whole before any cell runs, so a type error in the last cell stops the build before the first one runs.

docs.title: Keeping the cells
docs.text:
--emit after keeps every cell and writes its output after it, between two comments a Markdown preview does not display:

```hql id=todo
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```
<!-- hql:output id=todo hash=9c9f41e99b94 status=ok -->
- Leaves of Grass
- The Common Reader
- The Hobbit
<!-- /hql:output -->

With --in-place that rewrites the source itself, the way a notebook saves its outputs, and the next render replaces what is between the markers. The opening marker records the cell's id, a hash of its code and of the code of every cell it reads, and its status. An output whose hash differs from the cell's current one is stale, and an editor can say so without running anything.

--cell <id> runs one cell and the cells it reads, and rewrites only its output. --envelope json prints the built document and a record per cell — its id, span, hash, type, status, output and reports — for an editor to read.

docs.title: Cells that maintain a vault
docs.text:
Design only

This section describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these cells do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before they ship.

A vault's upkeep is a set of questions asked of the vault itself: which cards are related to this one, what does each category hold, which card does nothing link to. Each is a cell a card carries, and the hash in its saved output says when the answer is stale, so maintenance is a render, not a chore. A card of a vault's own wiki might end with these:

## Related

```hql#eval id=related
cards | semantic(this.title) | take(3) | map(h => h.value)
```

## Index

```hql#eval id=index
cards
| group(by = c => c.metadata.category)
| map(g => {category: g.key, cards: g.items | map(c => c.name)})
```

## Health

```hql#eval id=orphans
cards | filter(c => (c | downlinks | size) == 0) | map(c => c.name)
```

this is the card the cell is written in, so the related cards are the three nearest in meaning to its title, written below its body as links. A cell marked cached would keep its output until the hash of its code and its inputs changes, so a summary a model wrote (chapter 20) is computed once and read many times. The cell kinds exist today; this, cached and a semantic over a question the index was not built for are design direction.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 20 gives a language model the cards a query selected, runs an agent over them, and keeps the run as a value.

docs.title: 20. Agents and runs
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before it ships.

Most of the work around a language model is not the call itself. Choosing evidence, building the context, writing the prompt, giving the model tools, continuing a conversation and keeping what came back are dataflow, and HQL writes them as dataflow. Every stage is a typed value: what reached the model, what it called and what it answered are read the way a card is read.

The constructors in this chapter are pure and need no import. The steps that reach a model need import ai, which is how a program states that it may spend money and send text to a third party.

docs.title: An agent is a card
docs.text:
An agent is behaviour and configuration, written as a card. Its body is its instructions, and its agent header table configures it. This one is the reading-club vault's librarian.hmd:

---
title: Librarian
agent:
  model: default
  tools: [books_by]
  max_turns: 4
---
# Librarian

Answer questions about the club's shelf from the cards you are given and the
tools you have. Name the books you rely on. Say so when the shelf does not
answer the question.

Agent reads one from a card:

librarian = @[[librarian]] | Agent
librarian.tools

["books_by"]

A card is an agent only by saying it is one: Agent refuses a card with no agent table, and an unknown key in it, so a misspelt max_turn does not quietly select the default. model names a key of [ai.models] in the vault's hql.toml, never a provider, so a committed card does not fix a vendor:

[ai]
recordings = ".hql/runs"

[ai.models.default]
api = "messages"
endpoint = "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"
model = "claude-sonnet-5-5"
max_tokens = 1024
temperature = 0

docs.title: Context and prompt
docs.text:
Context(label) turns values into what a model reads: one item per element, each written as markdown writes it, with where it came from:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| map(i => {label: i.label, source: i.provenance.name})

[{label: "unread", source: "leaves-of-grass"}, {label: "unread", source: "the-common-reader"}, {label: "unread", source: "the-hobbit"}]

A context is a Seq<ContextItem>, so contexts are combined with concat and narrowed with filter, like any other sequence. A ranking from chapter 18 keeps each hit's score and retrieval in its item, so cards | semantic(question) | take(10) | Context("evidence") is evidence that says how it was found.

Prompt(instructions) puts the task in front of the context. Its rendered field is the text exactly as sent:

p = cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| Context("unread")
| Prompt("Which unread book should the club start with?")

p.rendered

Which unread book should the club start with?

## unread

Source: leaves-of-grass

# Leaves of Grass

Poems by [[walt-whitman]], revised and enlarged for the rest of his life.

Source: the-common-reader

# The Common Reader

Essays by [[virginia-woolf]] on reading, written for readers rather than critics.

Source: the-hobbit

# The Hobbit

A novel by [[jrr-tolkien]]. A hobbit is talked into an adventure and comes home changed.

docs.title: Tools are functions
docs.text:
A tool is a named HQL function. Tool records its name, a description and the JSON Schema of its parameters, derived from their types:

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")

Tool {name: "books_by", description: "The titles on the shelf by one author", parameters: {"properties":{"author":{"type":"string"}},"required":["author"],"type":"object"}}

A tool is pure. While the harness evaluates one for a model, every effectful step is refused, so no path through the function reaches a file, a network or another model. The tools a run is given must be exactly those the agent's card lists: the card is where a reader learns what an agent can do.

docs.title: Running an agent
docs.text:
run(agent, tools = …) executes the agent over a context or a prompt until it stops, and returns a Run. This program is pick.hql:

import ai

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

librarian = @[[librarian]] | Agent

pick =
    cards
    | filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
    | Context("unread")
    | Prompt("Which unread book should the club start with?")
    | run(librarian, tools = [Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")])

pick.result

"Start with The Common Reader. It is the only unread book by Virginia Woolf, and the club has already read A Room of One's Own and is reading Mrs Dalloway, so it completes the club's Woolf."

The answer is one field among many. The harness never collapses a run into the text the model last wrote:

pick.calls | map(c => {tool: c.tool, status: c.status, output: c.output})

[{output: "[\"A Room of One's Own\",\"Mrs Dalloway\",\"The Common Reader\"]", status: "ok", tool: "books_by"}]

turns is the conversation, stop says why it ended — end, max_tokens, max_turns or refused — and model and usage are what the provider reported, not what configuration asked for. trace puts everything that happened in one order:

pick | trace | map(e => e.kind)

["prompt", "request", "response", "tool_call", "request", "response", "stop"]

docs.title: Continuing and delegating
docs.text:
A Run never changes. ask(message) continues its conversation with the same agent and tools, and returns a new run whose parent is the first:

why = pick | ask("What did you rely on?")
why.result

"The books_by tool listed three Woolf titles, and the card for The Common Reader is the only one marked todo."

delegate(agent, task) starts a fresh conversation for another agent, given the first run's context and its result. An agent named in a card's agents: list is offered to the model as a tool of that name, so a model may delegate by itself; each child run is kept in children, and delegation stops at depth three.

remember(name) writes a run's result, or a string, as a card in the vault's [ai.memory] dir. Memory is cards: writing it is one explicit step, and reading it is a query like any other.

docs.title: Recordings: a run that answers again
docs.text:
A program that reaches a model would answer differently on every evaluation. HQL keeps each response as a recording, keyed by the SHA-256 of the request it answers, under the vault's [ai] recordings directory. --ai chooses what may happen:

Mode What it does replay the default: answers from recordings only, and never reaches a network record sends what is not recorded yet, and records it live always sends

The mode is never read from hql.toml, so spending money is always a choice made on the command line. Record once, and the same program then evaluates offline, byte for byte:

$ hql --vault . --ai record run pick.hql
"Start with The Common Reader. …"
$ hql --vault . run pick.hql
"Start with The Common Reader. …"

A request with no recording is a diagnostic, not an empty answer:

evaluation failure: no recording for this request (5e10ae23…); run with --ai record
  --> pick.hql:13:7
