hql check checks the whole program, its type is Run, and no model is reached. Committed recordings make a document that calls a model as reproducible as one that does not.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A cell is a program, so a cell may run an agent, and the document around it is the prompt. Chapter 21 writes a document whose cells retrieve evidence, run the librarian over the draft they sit in, and save the answer where it was asked.

docs.title: 21. Agents inside documents
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: these programs do not run against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before it ships.

Chapter 20 ran an agent from a program. This chapter runs one from inside the document that asks the question. The knowledge, the prompt, the program that assembles the prompt and the answer then sit in one file, each visible, each editable, each a value a later cell can read. The document is examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd, rendered against the tutorial vault like the reading list of chapter 19.

docs.title: The document is the harness
docs.text:
Two bindings reach a cell from the host. cell is the cell being rendered, whose logs channel the logging page wrote to. this is the card the cell is written in, as it stands when the render starts: its header, its prose, and every output a previous render saved into it.

The prose of a cell's section, from the nearest heading above the cell down to the cell itself, is the default instructions of every Prompt the cell builds. The question is written once, as prose a reader reads, and the cell below it carries only the program that gathers the evidence.

hql render --emit after --in-place writes each cell's output back into the document, between the markers of chapter 19. The opening marker's hash covers the cell's code and the code of every cell it reads; a cell that reads this also covers the document's text, so its output is stale after every edit of the prose around it. That is the loop this chapter is about: edit the draft, render, read the answer, edit again.

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
---
title: Next meeting
---
# Next meeting

Notes for the club's next meeting, built from the shelf with
`hql --vault examples/tutorial render`.

```hql id=books hidden
cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
```

## Candidates

The books nobody has finished.

```hql id=unread
books
| filter(c => c.metadata.status == "todo")
| sort(by = c => c.title)
| map(c => c.title)
```

## Evidence

What the shelf holds on the question the club keeps returning to.

```hql id=evidence hidden
import semantic
cards | semantic("which unread book suits a reading club") | take(3) | Context("evidence")
```

## What should we read next?

Pick one unread book for the next meeting, and say why. The candidates and
the evidence are in this draft; rely on them and on the shelf.

```hql#eval id=pick
import ai

fn books_by(author: String) : List<String> =
    cards | filter(c => c.metadata.author == author) | map(c => c.title) | List

[this]
| Context("draft")
| concat(evidence)
| run(@[[librarian]] | Agent, tools = [Tool(books_by, "The titles on the shelf by one author")])
```

## What happened

```hql#eval id=trace
pick | trace | map(e => e.kind)
```

## Remembered

```hql id=note hidden
pick | remember("next-meeting-pick")
```

```hql#eval
cards | filter(c => c.path | starts_with("memory/")) | map(c => c.title)
```

The first two cells run against the current binary; they are the reading list of chapter 19 again. The rest is the subject of this chapter.

docs.title: Evidence by meaning
docs.text:
The evidence cell is a ranking of chapter 18 turned into a context. Each hit becomes one item, and the item keeps what the hit knew: its score, and the retrieval that produced it, in its provenance. Evidence that reaches a model says how it was found:

evidence | map(i => {source: i.provenance.name, score: i.score})

[{score: 0.3127, source: "the-common-reader"}, {score: 0.2904, source: "club"}, {score: 0.2851, source: "leaves-of-grass"}]

The question is a literal because the vault's index answers the questions it was built for, as chapter 18 explains; a question the index lacks is a diagnostic naming the build command, not an empty context.

docs.title: The agent reads the draft
docs.text:
[this] | Context("draft") is a context of one item: the document as it stands, written as Markdown, with the card's name and path as its provenance. concat(evidence) appends the ranking. The run step builds the prompt from the section's prose and both contexts, and the rendered prompt opens with the question the reader just read:

Pick one unread book for the next meeting, and say why. The candidates and
the evidence are in this draft; rely on them and on the shelf.

## draft

Source: next-meeting

# Next meeting
…

## evidence

Source: the-common-reader
…

The run's result is written after the cell, and the next cell reads the run itself, not its text:

```hql#eval id=pick
…
```
<!-- hql:output id=pick hash=3b91c0e4d2a7 status=ok -->
Start with The Common Reader. It is the only unread book by Virginia Woolf,
the club has read A Room of One's Own and is reading Mrs Dalloway, and the
draft lists it among the candidates.
<!-- /hql:output -->

["prompt", "request", "response", "tool_call", "request", "response", "stop"]

Change the prose above the cell, "say why" to "say why, in one sentence", and the cell's hash no longer matches its saved output. An editor shows the answer as stale without running anything; the next render asks again, with the new instructions and the draft as it now stands, which includes the previous answer. The agent reads what it wrote last time, as a value among the others.

docs.title: Memory is cards
docs.text:
remember(name) writes a run's result as a card in the vault's [ai.memory] directory, here memory/next-meeting-pick.hmd, with the run's id in its header so the card names the run that wrote it. Memory is cards: writing it is one explicit step, and reading it is a query like any other, which is what the last cell does. On the next render, cards holds the memory card and this holds the saved pick, so the document reads what it wrote.

In replay mode, the default, remember succeeds only when the card already holds the same content, so a committed vault renders without writing. Under --ai record or --ai live it writes.

docs.title: The editor loop
docs.text:
A request a run makes can be answered by three answerers, and every answer is a recording under the hash of the request, so a document rendered later reads all three alike. A provider answers over HTTP, as chapter 20 configured. A headless session of an agent host answers when the model entry names one. And under --ai host, a request with no recording is not sent anywhere: it waits, and whoever is driving the program answers it. In an editor that is the agent the user is already chatting with.

$ hql --vault examples/tutorial --ai host render --emit after --in-place examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd
$ hql --vault examples/tutorial ai pending
5e10ae23…  messages  next-meeting.hmd:31  pick
$ hql --vault examples/tutorial ai answer 5e10ae23… --text "Start with The Common Reader. …"
$ hql --vault examples/tutorial render examples/notebook/next-meeting.hmd

hql ai pending lists each waiting request with its key, the wire format its answer is written in, and the request itself: the agent's instructions, the conversation, and the tools offered with their schemas. hql ai answer writes the answer as a recording marked answered_by: host, so a reader of the document can tell a provider's answer from one a person's chat gave. The second render replays it. Committed recordings make the document a procedure the chat executed once and anyone can read again.

edit the draft ──► render ──► request waits ──► chat answers ──► recording
      ▲                                                             │
      └───────────────── read the saved output ◄────────────────────┘

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Every card in this chapter was in one vault. Chapter 22 asks what the same steps are over a web of them.

docs.title: 22. The hyper web
docs.text:
Design only

This chapter describes functionality that is not in the current release. It is written as if it existed: nothing in it runs against the current binary, and names, types and outputs may change before any of it ships. It is the direction the rest of the book points in, stated so that the direction can be read, questioned and changed.

A vault is one namespace: a tree of cards, closed by construction, in which every [[name]] resolves or is reported. The chapters of Part III queried, drew, ranked and ran agents over one such tree. This chapter asks what each of those steps is over many trees, authored and served independently, and what a reader is when the trees are read by programs and agents as much as by people.

docs.title: Namespaces beyond one tree
docs.text:
A reference may name a namespace: [[club:dune]] is the card dune in the namespace bound as club. The binding lives in the vault's configuration, never in a card, so a card cannot reach a namespace by mentioning it, and removing the binding breaks every link that used it, visibly. A prefix is a permission.

[namespaces.club]
root = "../reading-club"

[namespaces.lit]
url = "https://lit.example.org/"

HQL already has the local half of this. source("club") in chapter 16 is a vault bound by configuration, with its own cards and graph, and a relation across the two is a join. A namespace bound to a URL is the same source whose provider is a server; the program is unchanged:

lit = source("lit")
lit.cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book") | size

The rule the design rests on is no silent dereference: rendering, checking and linting make no network call, and a program that reads a remote namespace does so in a step the host sees and may refuse, as it sees and may refuse source(http(…)) today.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider is anything that returns a card for a path: the vault's own folder, another folder, a web server that speaks plain HTTP and publishes a route description so a client does not guess its layout, a database holding cards as rows. The card's name is the same whichever provider answers, so a program over cards is a program over a web of vaults, and where a card is stored stays out of every reference to it.

What arrives from another provider is untrusted. A remote card's header is Data, as every tree from outside a program is, and it becomes a typed value at a boundary of chapter 11, where the program states what it requires and the rest is refused or kept as Data. A card of a namespace carries the namespace in its provenance, and so does every value derived from it: a hit, a context item, a run.

docs.title: Retrieval over the web
docs.text:
semantic over a namespace is the provider's index answering a question it holds, with its model, metric and approximation reported in the ranking's retrieval, as chapter 18 reports them for a local index. Two namespaces are two rankings, and a program that combines them does so explicitly, by score within a retrieval or by a join across them, because a score is evidence relative to one index and means nothing against another's.

import semantic

here  = cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3)
there = source("lit").cards | semantic("a creature and its maker") | take(3)
[here, there] | emit | Context("evidence")

Each item of that context says which namespace it came from, which index ranked it and how. Knowledge semantics becomes a way to query the web: a question in words, answered with cards and the evidence for each, rather than with pages to read.

docs.title: Agents reading agents
docs.text:
An agent is a card, so a namespace can serve one, and a document in one vault can run the librarian of another. delegate across a binding is a run whose child ran elsewhere, kept in children with its provenance, and whose trace records the delegation as an event like any other. The rules of chapter 20 do not change at the boundary: a child run is bounded in depth, every request is recorded under its hash, and a tool stays pure wherever it is evaluated.

import ai

review = cards | lexical("influence") | Context("claims") | run(@[[librarian]] | Agent)
second = review | delegate(@[[lit:reviewer]] | Agent, "Check the claims against your shelf.")
second.trace | filter(e => e.kind == "delegate") | map(e => e.data.namespace)

An agent that reads another agent's run reads a value: the prompt it was given, the tools it called, the answer it gave, and where each piece came from. A conversation between agents is a tree of such values, and a program queries it with the steps of chapter 6.

docs.title: A reader who asks
docs.text:
The same card is served to a person in a browser, to a tool that lints it, and to an agent building a context, from one source and in one format. A site that is a vault answers a question the way a document of chapter 21 does: with a run whose evidence is the site's own cards, whose trace says which cards were read, and whose answer carries their names. The reader asks instead of browsing, and what comes back is not a page but a value with its provenance attached, which the reader, or the reader's agent, may query further.

None of this needs a new language. It needs bindings in configuration, providers that answer by path, and the discipline the earlier chapters already hold: every step typed, every effect explicit, every value carrying where it came from.

docs.title: Where to go from here
docs.text: You have met the whole language, in three parts. The language: values and data, collections and functions, modules, questions in the style of SQL, streams, formats, data read and written through endpoints, the types a program declares and the boundary where data becomes typed, and the tools around it. Data flows: the pipeline, its phases, its unit of execution, and the systems it will connect. Knowledge and AI: a vault that is a namespace, its graph, retrieval by meaning, documents that compute themselves, agents whose runs are values, documents that run them, and the web they point at. The reference states each shipped part precisely, and the examples are where the next part is designed.

docs.title: 2. Data types
docs.text: Every value in HQL has a type, and the checker knows it before the program runs. This chapter meets the types values are built from: the scalars Int, Float, Decimal, String and Bool, and Data, the tree JSON and YAML are made of. Each has a page of its own; this one tries them in the REPL first.

docs.title: Trying values in the REPL
docs.text:
hql repl reads one input at a time, evaluates it and prints the value. A binding is kept for the inputs after it, and :type asks for a type without evaluating anything:

$ hql repl
hql 0.5.0. `:help` for commands, `:quit` to leave.
hql> pages = 412
()
hql> pages / 3
137
hql> pages % 3
1
hql> :type pages
Int
hql> title = "Dune"
()
hql> title.upper()
"DUNE"
hql> :type title
String
hql> fmt("{} has {} pages", title, pages)
"Dune has 412 pages"
hql> :quit

412 is an Int, so / divides whole numbers and drops the remainder, and % gives the remainder. "Dune" is a String, and title.upper() calls a function of String on it. fmt writes values into text, one {} each.

The same programs run with hql eval, as every program in this book does:

pages = 412
title = "Dune"
fmt("{} has {} pages", title, pages)

"Dune has 412 pages"

docs.title: A type is checked, not guessed
docs.text:
Each operation says which types it takes. An Int and a String do not add, and the checker rejects the program before it runs:

412 + "pages"

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands
 --> <expression>:1:7
  |
1 | 412 + "pages"
  |       ^^^^^^^

There is no implicit conversion between types, except that an Int beside a Decimal widens to one. str writes a value as text, and float turns an Int into a Float:

412.str()

"412"

hql check prints a program's type without evaluating it:

$ hql check - <<< '412 / 3'
Int

docs.title: The types, one page each
docs.text:
Type What it holds Page Int a whole number, 64 bits Int Float a binary floating-point number, written 2.5f Float Decimal an exact decimal number, written 2.50 Decimal String text String Bool true or false Bool Data a tree of records, lists and scalars Data Option<T> a T, or nothing Option

Braces write three different things — a set, a Data record and, where one is declared, a map — and sets, Data and maps tells them apart. Lists, sets and maps as collections, and the steps they share, are chapter 3.

docs.title: Bool
docs.text:
A Bool is true or false. Comparisons give one, and and, or and not combine them:

3 < 4 and not (1 > 2)

true

and and or are connectives of the language, so the right side is evaluated only when the left side does not decide the answer.

A Bool is not a number, and compares only with another Bool:

true == 1

check error[type-mismatch]: `Eq` for Bool compares with Bool, not Int
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | true == 1
  | ^^^^^^^^^

A condition must be a Bool. a given condition otherwise b chooses a value by one:

pages = 412
"long" given pages > 300 otherwise "short"

"long"

A Bool is a Scalar but not Orderable: true < false means nothing.

docs.title: Data: records and lists
docs.text: The values JSON and YAML are made of — records of named fields, lists, and scalar leaves — are one type in HQL, Data. This page does with Data what jq does with JSON: build it, read into it, reshape it, and write it back out.

docs.title: A tree of values
docs.text:
A data literal is written in braces, with a key, a colon and a value per field. Values may be scalars, lists, or other records:

{title: "Dune", author: {name: "Frank Herbert", born: 1920}, tags: ["desert", "spice"]}

{author: {born: 1920, name: "Frank Herbert"}, tags: ["desert", "spice"], title: "Dune"}

A key that is not an identifier is quoted: {"first name": "Ada"}. The record prints with its keys in order, so the same tree always prints the same way.

The colon is what makes braces a record. The empty record is {:}; {} without a colon is the empty set, as {1, 2} is a set of two. So d : Data = {:} holds an empty record, and d : Data = {} is a type error: {} is a Set<Never>, which a Set<Int> binding accepts and a Data one does not.

docs.title: Reading a field
docs.text:
A path reads into the tree, one key per step:

book = {title: "Dune", author: {name: "Frank Herbert", born: 1920}}
book.author.name

"Frank Herbert"

A key the tree does not have is not an error. The key belonged to whoever wrote the record, so nothing promised it, and reading it gives absence:

book = {title: "Dune"}
book.year

none

The type says so. Reading a key of a Data record gives an Option<Data>: a some holding a tree, or none. HQL has no null; a value that may be missing is an Option, and the program says what absence means where it matters.

year = {title: "Dune"}.year
match year {
    some(_) => "dated",
    none => "undated",
}

"undated"

docs.title: Asking what a leaf is
docs.text:
A leaf of a tree could be any scalar; the record did not say. Equality compares through that, so book.title == "Dune" is an ordinary question:

{title: "Dune"}.title == "Dune"

true

Arithmetic and ordering need to know the type. is(T) asks whether a value is a T, and a match arm with a type, some(Int n), both tests and reads it:

pages = {title: "Dune", pages: 412}.pages
match pages {
    some(Int n) => n * 2,
    _ => 0,
}

824

docs.title: Lists of records
docs.text:
A list of records is a List<Data>. map applies a function to every element, and x => x.title is a function written in place, a lambda:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books | map(b => b.title)

["Dune", "The Hobbit", "Leaves of Grass"]

| is a pipe: the value on its left is the input of the step on its right. filter keeps the elements a predicate accepts:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books
| filter(b => match b.pages { some(Int n) => n > 300, _ => false })
| map(b => b.title)

["Dune", "The Hobbit"]

To add up the page counts, the leaves become numbers first. somes drops the absent ones, of_type(Int) keeps the leaves that are integers and reads each as the Int it holds, and sum adds them:

books = [{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}, {title: "Leaves of Grass"}]
books
| map(b => b.pages)
| somes
| of_type(Int)
| sum

722

Each step is checked against the type the step before it produced. After of_type(Int) the list is a list of Int, which is what sum takes; without it the checker rejects sum over trees, before anything runs.

docs.title: Reshaping
docs.text:
A data literal can hold any expression, so map builds a new record from each old one:

books = [{title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert"}, {title: "Emma", author: "Jane Austen"}]
books | map(b => {book: b.title, by: b.author})

[{book: "Dune", by: "Frank Herbert"}, {book: "Emma", by: "Jane Austen"}]

merge combines two records. Every key of either is kept, and a key in both takes the value from the right:

merge({title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {pages: 896, edition: "illustrated"})

{edition: "illustrated", pages: 896, title: "Dune"}

docs.title: Writing it back out
docs.text:
A value is written in a presentation format by a step named for it. The result is text of that format — Json, Yaml, Csv, Markdown — and hql writes it as it is:

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}] | json

[
  {
    "pages": 412,
    "title": "Dune"
  },
  {
    "pages": 310,
    "title": "The Hobbit"
  }
]

{title: "Dune", pages: 412, tags: ["desert", "spice"]} | yaml

pages: 412
tags:
- desert
- spice
title: Dune

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}] | csv

pages,title
412,Dune
310,The Hobbit

A list of records becomes a table when it is built into one. Table takes the records as rows and columns names their fields in the order the table writes them; each format then writes the table in its own syntax, here a pipe table:

[{title: "Dune", pages: 412}, {title: "The Hobbit", pages: 310}]
| Table(columns = ["title", "pages"])
| markdown

| title      | pages |
| ---------- | ----- |
| Dune       | 412   |
| The Hobbit | 310   |

Chapter 8 is about formats in full.

A program writes its data as literals, reads it from a vault's documents, as chapter 16 does, or reads a JSON, YAML or CSV file with source, as chapter 9 does.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: How Data differs from a set and from a map, all three written in braces, is the next page. A Data list is one kind of collection. Chapter 3 meets the others — lists, sets and maps of typed values — and the steps that work on all of them.

docs.title: Decimal
docs.text:
A Decimal is an exact decimal number: an integer significand of up to 512 bits, about 154 digits, and a scale, the number of digits after the point, from 0 to 154. A number written with a decimal point is a Decimal, so arithmetic on it loses nothing to binary rounding:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3

true

The scale is kept for display. A sum or a difference has the larger scale of its operands, and a product the sum of their scales. Equality and order are by value, so 1.50 == 1.5 is true:

[1.50, 1.50 + 1.25, 1.50 * 1.5]

[1.50, 2.75, 2.250]

A literal keeps every digit it is written with, however many there are:

123456789012345678901234567890.123456789 + 0.000000001

123456789012345678901234567890.123456790

docs.title: Division and rounding
docs.text:
/ is exact where the quotient terminates, and otherwise rounded half to even to 100 significant digits. Division by zero is an evaluation error, as it is for an Int. round(x, places) rounds half to even to places digits after the point, and round(x) to a whole number:

[10 / 4.0, round(2 / 3.0, 4), round(2.345, 2), round(2.355, 2), round(2.5)]

[2.5, 0.6667, 2.34, 2.36, 2]

docs.title: Int, Float and Decimal
docs.text:
An Int beside a Decimal widens to one of scale 0, in arithmetic and in a comparison:

[12.50 * 3, 7 - 0.25]

[37.50, 6.75]

A Float does not mix with a Decimal: a binary float carries no exact decimal value, so the program says which conversion it means. decimal(x) reads an Int, or a Float by its shortest digits, as a Decimal; float(d) gives the nearest Float and int(d) the integer part:

1.5 + 2.0f

check error[type-mismatch]: a Decimal and a Float do not mix: write `decimal(x)` to read the Float as a Decimal, or `float(d)` to read the Decimal as a Float
 --> <expression>:1:7
  |
1 | 1.5 + 2.0f
  |       ^^^^

[decimal(0.1f) + 1.5, "12.50".to_decimal().unwrap_or(0.0)]

[1.6, 12.50]

JSON, YAML and CSV carry a Decimal without loss: a number read as a Decimal field keeps the digits it is written with, and a Decimal is written as a number with its digits and scale.

docs.title: Float
docs.text:
A Float is a 64-bit binary floating-point number, written with the suffix f: 0.5f, 6.02e23f, 2f. A number with a decimal point and no suffix is a Decimal. Arithmetic on two Float operands gives a Float:

7.0f / 2.0f

3.5

A binary fraction cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly, so a sum can be a little off:

0.1f + 0.2f

0.30000000000000004

That is why a Float is the wrong type for money; a Decimal holds an amount exactly as it is written.

An Int and a Float do not mix: 1 + 2.0f is a type error, and so is a Decimal beside a Float. float and int convert, the second truncating:

[1.float() + 2.0f, 3.9f.int().float()]

[3.0, 3.0]

docs.title: Int
docs.text:
An Int is a whole number: a signed 64-bit integer. Arithmetic on two Int operands gives an Int.

2 + 3 * 4

14

* and / bind tighter than + and -. Division truncates towards zero, and % is the remainder:

[7 / 2, -7 / 2, 7 % 3]

[3, -3, 1]

An Int that leaves the 64-bit range is an error, never a wrapped value:

9223372036854775807 + 1

execute failure[numeric-overflow]: numeric overflow
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | 9223372036854775807 + 1
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The math module adds what operators do not cover:

[2.pow(10), (-5).abs(), (-5).sign()]

[1024, 5, -1]

An Int is Orderable, so <, >, min, max and sort work on it, and it compares only with another Int. float turns it into a Float, and str into a String.

docs.title: Option: a value that may be missing
docs.text:
The reading club gives a book its rating when the book is done. A book still being read has no rating yet, so the club's notes have a field some records carry and others do not:

books = [
    {title: "Frankenstein", status: "done", rating: 5},
    {title: "Dune", status: "reading"},
    {title: "A Room of One's Own", status: "done", rating: 4},
]
books | map(b => b.rating)

[5, none, 4]

HQL has no null. A value that may be missing is an Option<T>: some(x), which holds an x, or none, which holds nothing. A present value prints as the value it holds, and an absent one as none.

docs.title: The type says so
docs.text:
Reading a field of a Data record gives an Option<Data>, whichever record it reads, because the type is known before any record is:

{title: "Dune"}.rating

Option<Data>

An Option is not the value it may hold. Adding to a rating that may be missing is a type error, reported before the program runs:

rating = {title: "Frankenstein", rating: 5}.rating
rating + 1

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands, or two values of a type implementing `Add`, not Option<Data>
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | rating + 1
  | ^^^^^^

The program says what a missing rating means, and the ways to say it follow.

docs.title: A value in place of none
docs.text:
unwrap_or(default) gives the value held, or default where there is none:

books | map(b => b.rating.unwrap_or(0))

[5, 0, 4]

There is no unwrap without a default. Every way out of an Option states what absence means.

docs.title: One answer for each case
docs.text:
match takes an Option apart. The some(r) arm binds the value held to r, the none arm covers the rest, and the checker rejects a match that leaves a case uncovered:

books | map(b => {
    book: b.title,
    verdict: match b.rating {
        some(r) => fmt("{} stars", r),
        none => "not rated yet",
    },
})

[{book: "Frankenstein", verdict: "5 stars"}, {book: "Dune", verdict: "not rated yet"}, {book: "A Room of One's Own", verdict: "4 stars"}]

is_some and is_none ask the question as a Bool, for a filter or a given:

books | filter(b => b.rating.is_none()) | map(b => b.title)

["Dune"]

docs.title: Only the values that are there
docs.text:
somes keeps the present values of a collection of options and drops the absent ones. The club's ratings so far are the ratings of the books it has finished:

books | map(b => b.rating) | somes

[5, 4]

docs.title: Comparing with a missing value
docs.text:
Equality compares through an Option: some(5) == 5 is true, and none is equal to no value. A book with no rating is not a five-star book:

books | filter(b => b.rating == 5) | map(b => b.title)

["Frankenstein"]

docs.title: Options from other places
docs.text:
A record field is one source of options; a step that may have no answer is another. to_int reads a String as an Int, and gives none where the text is not a number:

["412", "four", "310"] | map(s => s.to_int())

[412, none, 310]

A step applied to an Option is applied to the value held. map gives the result in a some, or none where there was nothing to apply it to; filter keeps a value that passes a test; and alternative gives a second option where the first is none:

[
    "412".to_int().map(n => n / 2),
    "four".to_int().map(n => n / 2),
    "1965".to_int().filter(y => y > 1900),
    "four".to_int().alternative("0".to_int()),
]

[206, none, 1965, 0]

max over an empty list, a position past the end of a string and a link to a card nobody has written are each an Option too, and each is handled the same way.

A missing value is not a failure. A computation that can fail gives a Result, ok or err, and chapter 10 meets it.

docs.title: Sets, Data and maps
docs.text:
Three kinds of value are written in braces, or hold keys and values, and they are easy to mix up. They are different types with different jobs:

Type What it is Written Set<T> distinct values of one type, with no positions {1, 2, 3} Data a tree of named fields of any types, the shape of JSON {title: "Dune", pages: 412} Map<K, V> keys of one type, each to a value of one type Map(["dune"], [412])

docs.title: The colon tells braces apart
docs.text:
Braces holding values are a set; braces holding key: value entries are Data. The colon is the only thing that tells them apart, and the empty forms keep it: {} is the empty set and {:} the empty Data.

{3, 1, 3, 2}

{3, 1, 2}

{title: "Dune", pages: 412}

{pages: 412, title: "Dune"}

{}

{}

{:}

{:}

A set keeps each value once. A Data record prints its keys in order, so the same tree always prints the same way.

{} has a definite meaning, the empty set, so it is not an empty record:

d : Data = {}
d

check error[type-mismatch]: `d` is declared Data but its value is Set<Never>
 --> <expression>:1:12
  |
1 | d : Data = {}
  |            ^^

{} is a Set<Never>: a set with no elements, and so no element type yet. A declared set type gives it one:

seen : Set<Int> = {}
seen | size

0

docs.title: Data is not a map
docs.text:
Data is the type of values whose shape is not known to the program: what a JSON or YAML document decodes to. A record's fields may hold different types, a number beside a text beside a list, and nesting goes as deep as the document does. It is not a hash map, and not a Map<String, Any>.

A Map<K, V> is a typed mapping: every key is a K and every value a V. The constructor pairs a list of keys with a list of values:

Map(["dune", "emma"], [412, 474])

Map {"dune": 412, "emma": 474}

Map(["dune", "emma"], [412, 474]).get("dune")

412

So the three answer different needs: a set, which values; a map, which value for each key, all of one type; Data, whatever structure arrived.

docs.title: {:} is Data, or a declared map
docs.text:
{:} has no type of its own. Where nothing says otherwise it is the empty Data; where a map type is declared for it, it is that empty map:

Written Type Value {:} with nothing around it Data the empty Data record, printed {:} d : Data = {:} Data the same m : Map<String, Int> = {:} Map<String, Int> an empty map, equal to Map<String, Int>([], []) m : SortedMap<String, Int> = {:}, or OrderedMap that map type an empty map of that kind f({:}) where f takes a Map<String, Int> Map<String, Int> an empty map 
counts : Map<String, Int> = {:}
counts == Map<String, Int>([], [])

true

Data is the default, and a declared Map, OrderedMap or SortedMap turns it into that empty map. An empty literal carries no information of its own, so the type around it decides: HQL infers a type while the literal says enough, and asks for an explicit one where it does not.

This holds for the empty literal only. A non-empty keyed literal is always Data, and binding it to a declared map type is a type error:

m : Map<String, Int> = {a: 1}
m

check error[type-mismatch]: `m` is declared Map<String, Int> but its value is Data
 --> <expression>:1:24
  |
1 | m : Map<String, Int> = {a: 1}
  |                        ^^^^^^

A non-empty map is built with the constructor, Map(["a"], [1]).

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Chapter 3 uses lists, sets and maps as collections, and the steps they share.

docs.title: String
docs.text:
A String is text, written in double quotes. Its functions are called on it with a dot:

"Ada Lovelace".upper()

"ADA LOVELACE"

Its length counts characters, not bytes:

"héllo".length()

5

A position reads one character. It may be past the end, so it gives an Option<String>, printed as the character when it is present:

"Dune"[0]

"D"

+ on two strings is concatenation. Both operands are strings: "a" + 1 is a type error. fmt writes values of any type into a template, one {} each, and join puts a list of strings together with a separator:

["Dune" + " (1965)", fmt("{} has {} pages", "Dune", 412), ["a", "b", "c"].join(", ")]

["Dune (1965)", "Dune has 412 pages", "a, b, c"]

split, trim, replace_all, starts_with, contains and the rest are in the string module, visible in every program:

"  Frankenstein  ".trim().starts_with("Frank")

true

A String is Orderable, in the order of its characters, so a list of them sorts. Any value becomes text with str.

docs.title: 4. Functions
docs.text: A function is a value of a function type. It can be bound to a name, passed to a step, returned from another function, and written once for every type it works on. This page meets lambdas and function types; the pages after it declare functions with fn.

docs.title: Lambdas and their types
docs.text:
n => n * 2 is a lambda. Written as an argument, it takes its parameter's type from the step it is passed to. Written on its own, it states the type:

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
[412, 280] | map(double)

[824, 560]

A function's type is written with an arrow: Int -> Int, (Int, Int) -> Int.

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
double

Int -> Int

A lambda's body is one expression. A function whose value takes several steps is declared with fn, whose body may be a block of them.

docs.title: Calling a function
docs.text:
f(x) calls a function. Piping into one calls it too: x | f is f(x), and x | f(y) is f(x, y), the piped value filling the first parameter.

double = (n: Int) => n * 2
280 | double

560

docs.title: The pages of this chapter
docs.text: Page What it covers Declaring a function fn, typed parameters and a result, recursion, functions taken and returned, variadic parameters Function bodies the two body forms, = expr and the block { … }, and the rules a block follows Generic functions type parameters, and the bounds a call is checked against Aliases and holes := names a pipeline fragment, and _ leaves an argument open

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: A program's functions sit beside its expressions. Chapter 5 puts functions into modules of their own: files that a program imports, with public and private declarations.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Most small functions are a pipeline fragment with a name. := defines an alias, and the checker writes its type: the input is the most general one the fragment accepts, and each parameter takes the type of the step argument it fills.

top(n) := sort | take(n)
[412, 280, 310, 145] | top(2)

[145, 280]

hql check prints the signature it wrote:

top(n) := sort | take(n)
1

top : (Collection<T>, Int) -> List<T> where T : Orderable
Int

docs.title: Holes
docs.text:
A call with _ for an argument is a function of the arguments left open — a partial application:

fn add(a: Int, b: Int) : Int = a + b
[1, 2, 3] | map(add(10, _))

[11, 12, 13]

A hole is a whole argument. _ + 1 is not a hole, and a lambda, n => n + 1, writes that function.

docs.title: Function bodies
docs.text:
A function's body takes one of two forms: an expression after =, or a block in braces, written without =. The two forms are equally general: any function may take either, at any result type, and both declare the same function.

fn doubled_sum(xs: List<Int>) : Int = xs | map(x => x * 2) | sum

fn doubled_sum_block(xs: List<Int>) : Int {
    xs
    | map(x => x * 2)
    | sum
}

[doubled_sum([1, 2, 3]), doubled_sum_block([1, 2, 3])]

[12, 12]

A pipeline is an expression, so = xs | f | g binds the whole pipeline. In a block, a pipeline continues over several lines, each opening with |. A body longer than one line is written as a block.

docs.title: The value block
docs.text:
A value block is zero or more bindings, name = expr, one per line, followed by one final expression. The final expression is the function's value and has the declared result type:

fn label(pages: Int) : String {
    days = (pages + 39) / 40
    kind = "short" given pages < 200 otherwise "long"
    fmt("{} ({} days)", kind, days)
}

[145, 412] | map(label)

["short (4 days)", "long (11 days)"]

Each binding names one step of the computation. The steps may call other functions, and the final line combines them:

fn area(width: Float, height: Float) : Float {
    w = width
    h = height
    w * h
}

fn triangle(base: Float, height: Float) : Float {
    whole = area(base, height)
    whole / 2.0f
}

[area(2.0f, 3.0f), triangle(5.0f, 5.0f)]

[6.0, 12.5]

A value block takes any result type. A block returning Seq<Int> without yield is a value block, and its last line is the sequence it returns:

fn even_squares(xs: List<Int>) : Seq<Int> {
    evens = xs | filter(x => x % 2 == 0)
    evens | map(x => x * x)
}

List(even_squares([1, 2, 3, 4]))

[4, 16]

docs.title: A block's scope
docs.text:
A binding is in scope from the line after it to the end of its block, and nowhere else. A binding inside a block shadows a name outside it without changing that name. A lambda on the final line captures the block's bindings, and takes its parameter type from the declared result:

k = 100

fn adder(n: Int) : Int -> Int {
    k = n * 10
    x => x + k
}

add = adder(2)
[add(1), add(5), k]

[21, 25, 100]

A block's bindings are not visible after the function:

fn area(w: Float, h: Float) : Float {
    a = w * h
    a
}
a

check error[unknown-name]: `a` is not bound
 --> <expression>:5:1
  |
5 | a
  | ^
  = help: did you mean `abs`?

docs.title: The iterating block
docs.text:
A block containing yield is an iterating block. It holds bindings, yield expr and for name in collection { … }, one per line, and produces its values in the order each yield is reached. Its result type is Seq<T>, which ends, or Stream<T>, which need not, and each yielded value is a T:

fn countdown(from: Int) : Seq<Int> {
    for n in range(0, from) {
        yield from - n
    }
}

List(countdown(3))

[3, 2, 1]

Chapter 7 is about iterating functions and the streams they produce.

docs.title: What a block may not be
docs.text:
A block ends either in a final expression or in yields, never in both and never in neither. The parser rejects each of these as a syntax failure.

A block of bindings alone has no value:

fn one() : Int {
    x = 1
}

one()

parse failure[unexpected-token]: a block ends in a value or yields; this one holds only bindings
 --> <expression>:1:16
  |
1 | fn one() : Int {
  |                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A block that yields holds no expression on a line of its own:

fn numbers() : Seq<Int> {
    yield 1
    2
}

List(numbers())

parse failure[unexpected-token]: a block that yields holds no expression on a line of its own
 --> <expression>:3:5
  |
3 |     2
  |     ^

for belongs to an iterating block:

fn total(xs: List<Int>) : Int {
    for x in xs {
        y = x
    }
    0
}

total([1, 2])

parse failure[unexpected-token]: `for` belongs to an iterating block; a value block is bindings and a final expression
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 |     for x in xs {
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

= { begins a record or set literal, never a block, so a binding inside it does not parse:

fn one() : Int = {
    x = 1
    x
}

one()

parse failure[unexpected-token]: expected `}` after collection elements, found `=`
 --> <expression>:2:7
  |
2 |     x = 1
  |       ^

docs.title: Wherever a function is declared
docs.text:
A function has one shape wherever it is declared, and its body takes either form in each place: at the top level of a program, in a module (chapter 5), as a receiver function taking self (receiver modules), and as a trait's default body or an implementation's function (traits).

A lambda's body stays one expression; a function that needs a block is declared with fn.

docs.title: Declaring a function
docs.text:
fn declares a named function: a name, typed parameters, a result type and a body. fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int gives days the type (Int, Int) -> Int.

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = (pages + per_day - 1) / per_day
[days(412, 40), days(280, 40)]

[11, 7]

Every parameter has a type and the result type is written. Each call is checked against them before the program runs:

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = (pages + per_day - 1) / per_day
days("412", 40)

check error[type-mismatch]: this argument is String, and parameter `pages` takes Int
 --> <expression>:2:6
  |
2 | days("412", 40)
  |      ^^^^^

The body after = is one expression. A body may also be a block of named steps, in braces; Function bodies covers both forms.

docs.title: A function by its name
docs.text:
Naming a declared function where a function is expected passes it as a value, xs | map(f). Its name is bound before its body is checked, so it may call itself:

fn factorial(n: Int) : Int = 1 given n <= 1 otherwise n * factorial(n - 1)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5] | map(factorial)

[1, 2, 6, 24, 120]

docs.title: Functions taken and returned
docs.text:
A parameter may have a function type, and so may the result. A returned function keeps the values it captured:

fn adder(k: Int) : Int -> Int = n => n + k
fn twice(f: Int -> Int, x: Int) : Int = f(f(x))
twice(adder(3), 30)

36

docs.title: Variadic parameters
docs.text:
A last parameter written ...T collects any number of trailing arguments into a list:

fn total(xs: ...Int) : Int = xs | sum
[total(), total(1, 2), total(1, 2, 3, 4)]

[0, 3, 10]

docs.title: A result that may be missing
docs.text:
Option<T> is the result type of a function whose value may be absent. some(x) and none build one, match takes one apart, and somes keeps the present values of a collection:

fn rating_of(r: Int) : Option<Int> = some(r) given r > 0 otherwise none
[5, 0, 4] | map(rating_of) | somes

[5, 4]

Option has the rest of Option's operations.

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
A function written once for every type names a type parameter, one capital letter in angle brackets after its name. Each call fills it from its arguments:

fn first<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | reduce((a, b) => a)
first(["Dune", "Emma"])

"Dune"

The same function over a list of numbers gives an Option<Int>:

fn first<T>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | reduce((a, b) => a)
first([412, 280])

Option<Int>

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text:
Inside the body T is a type of its own: the body may rely only on what the parameter promises. A bound, T : Orderable, promises an order, so the body may sort or find a minimum, and each call is checked against the bound:

fn shortest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | min
shortest([412, 280, 310])

280

fn shortest<T : Orderable>(xs: List<T>) : Option<T> = xs | min
shortest([{1}, {2}])

check error[type-mismatch]: `shortest` needs T : Orderable, and T is Set<Int> here
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | shortest([{1}, {2}])
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A bound is a type or a trait. Traits declares traits of a program's own and bounds by them.

docs.title: 5. Modules
docs.text: A module is a named unit of declarations — functions, types, traits and bindings — kept in a file of its own. A program reaches a module's declarations by importing it. This page writes a module and imports it; the pages after it cover receiver modules, visibility, and how a name resolves.

docs.title: A module is a file under a module root
docs.text:
A workspace module is an HQL file under a module root, named by its position under the root: lib/club/reading.hql is the module club.reading, and lib/club/mod.hql would be club. The roots come from hql.toml:

[modules]
roots = ["lib"]

or from --modules lib on the command line. The tutorial vault configures lib/ as its root, and keeps the book's modules there.

Every module file opens with its name, which is checked against the file's place under its root. This is lib/club/reading.hql:

/// Reading plans: how long a book takes at a number of pages a day.
module club.reading

private fn rounded_up(n: Int, d: Int) : Int = (n + d - 1) / d

/// Days to read `pages` at `per_day` pages a day; a part day counts as one.
fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = rounded_up(pages, per_day)

/// Days to read every book of `shelf`, one after another.
fn days_for_all(shelf: List<Int>, per_day: Int) : Int {
    each = shelf | map(pages => days(pages, per_day))
    each | sum
}

A /// line is a doc string: it documents the declaration after it, and hql help club.reading prints it. private keeps rounded_up inside the module, which visibility covers.

docs.title: Importing a module
docs.text:
import club.reading makes the module visible under its last segment, reading, and its functions are called through that name:

import club.reading

[reading.days(412, 40), reading.days(280, 40), reading.days_for_all([412, 280, 310], 40)]

[11, 7, 26]

import a.b as c makes it visible under c instead:

import club.reading as plan

plan.days(412, 40)

11

A module's function is a value like any other, and takes holes:

import club.reading

[412, 280] | map(reading.days(_, 40))

[11, 7]

Imports sit at the head of a source unit, before its declarations and expressions. Two imports may not share a local name:

import club.reading
import club.titles as reading
1

check error[unknown-name]: `reading` already names the module `club.reading` here; import `club.titles` under another name with `as`
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | import club.titles as reading
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A module that is not imported is not visible, however it is spelled:

reading.days(412, 40)

check error[unknown-name]: `reading` is not bound
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | reading.days(412, 40)
  | ^^^^^^^

docs.title: The standard modules
docs.text:
The standard library is modules of the same kind. The prelude is the list of modules every program imports without writing it: string, seq, math, option and result, among others. "a,b".split(",") calls the prelude's string.split. Other standard modules are imported by name:

import regex

regex.split("a1b22c", "[0-9]+")

["a", "b", "c"]

The reference has a page per standard module.

docs.title: The pages of this chapter
docs.text: Page What it covers Receiver modules module m for T, functions taking self, and value.f() calls Visibility public and private declarations, and a module's contract How names resolve import units, a unit's own names, ambiguity, and modules as closures

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: With functions and modules in hand, chapter 6 asks the questions SQL asks: where, order by, group by, and the aggregates.

docs.title: How names resolve
docs.text: Every module is an import unit: one scope in which its imports take effect and its names resolve. A program is an import unit of its own, the program module. An import makes a module visible in the importing unit and nowhere else.

docs.title: Imports are per unit
docs.text: A module's imports are its own. A module that imports math sees math, and a program that imports the module does not see math through it. The prelude, too, is the implicit import list of each unit separately.

docs.title: A unit's own names win
docs.text:
A declaration the unit writes itself wins over an imported declaration of the same name, in every spelling: an unqualified call, a pipeline step and a receiver call. The imported one stays reachable through its module. This program declares its own lower:

fn lower(s: String) : String = "mine"
[lower("ABC"), "ABC" | lower, string.lower("ABC")]

["mine", "mine", "abc"]

The program's lower takes no self, so the receiver spelling reaches nothing, and the prelude's lower is not reached in its place:

fn lower(s: String) : String = "mine"
"ABC".lower()

check error[unknown-name]: `lower` is this unit's own function, which takes no `self`, so `value.lower(…)` does not reach it and no import's `lower` over String is reached in its place; write `lower(value, …)`, or qualify the import's
 --> <expression>:2:1
  |
2 | "ABC".lower()
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A unit owns its own names, so a module that later gains a declaration of the same name cannot take one away from it. Which declaration wins does not depend on the order the declarations are written in.

docs.title: Two imports, one name
docs.text: Two imported declarations of one name, neither the unit's own, are an ambiguity, and the call naming them is a name error. Qualifying the call resolves it, titles.initials(s) or string.split(s, ","); the order of the imports never decides.

docs.title: A module is a closure
docs.text:
A free name in a module resolves through the module's own declarations and its own imports, and through nothing else. A module never sees the program module, and no module imports it. The bindings the host seeds into a program — vault, cards, stdin, stdout and the rest — are not bound in a module. What a module needs from a program reaches it as a parameter, a function argument or a trait bound:

module club.shelf

fn books(cards: Seq<Card>) : Seq<Card> = cards | filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")

A program calls it with its own cards, shelf.books(cards). A module written this way checks once, and means the same in every program that imports it.

docs.title: Imports form no cycle
docs.text: The import graph is acyclic: an import that closes a cycle is a name error, and the diagnostic names the cycle. The module name tree is not a dependency graph — club and club.reading see nothing of each other unless one imports the other. A child may import its parent; a parent importing its child is warned at the import. Two modules that need each other are resolved by moving the shared part into a module both import.

docs.title: Receiver modules
docs.text:
A module that names a type pattern after for, module club.titles for String, is a receiver module. Its functions take self as their first parameter, at the module's pattern, and once the module is imported they resolve as receiver calls, value.f(args), on every value the pattern fits. This is lib/club/titles.hql:

/// Receiver functions over a book's title.
module club.titles for String

/// The first letter of each word, `"The Hobbit".initials()` is `"TH"`.
fn initials(self) : String = self.words().map(w => w.slice(0, 1)).join("")

/// A shelf mark: the initials and the year, `"TH-1937"`.
fn shelf_mark(self, year: Int) : String = fmt("{}-{}", self.initials(), year)

self is written untyped: its type is the module's pattern, String. Inside the module, self.initials() calls the module's own receiver function.

import club.titles

["The Hobbit".initials(), "Dune".shelf_mark(1965), titles.initials("Mrs Dalloway")]

["TH", "D-1965", "MD"]

value.f(args) is module.f(value, args): the value fills self, and titles.initials("Mrs Dalloway") is the same call written with its module. A function declared without self takes no receiver and is called only through its module.

docs.title: Receiver calls throughout the book
docs.text:
The prelude's modules are receiver modules too: string is module string for String, so "Dune".upper() calls string.upper, and [1, 2].size() calls the collection's size. A receiver call is resolved by the value's type among the modules in scope, so two modules may declare one name over different types: "abc".contains("b") is the string's and [1, 2].contains(2) the collection's.

c.title without parentheses is a field read, not a call.

docs.title: A receiver function's body
docs.text:
A receiver function is a function, and its body takes either form. A block over self names its steps as any block does:

module counting for Int

fn twice(self) : Int {
    doubled = self * 2
    doubled
}

A program declares no receiver functions: self belongs to a module's pattern, and a program has none.

fn initials(self: String) : String = "TH"
"The Hobbit".initials()

parse failure[unexpected-token]: a function with a body takes its receiver at the module's pattern: write `self` untyped
 --> <expression>:1:19
  |
1 | fn initials(self: String) : String = "TH"
  |                   ^^^^^^

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text: A declaration inside a module is public unless it is marked private. A module's contract is its public declarations: what an importer reaches, and what the module promises to keep.

docs.title: Public by default
docs.text:
club.reading declares days and days_for_all unmarked, so both are public, and rounded_up marked private:

module club.reading

private fn rounded_up(n: Int, d: Int) : Int = (n + d - 1) / d

fn days(pages: Int, per_day: Int) : Int = rounded_up(pages, per_day)

days calls rounded_up inside the module. An importer reaches days, and rounded_up is not part of the contract:

import club.reading

reading.rounded_up(412, 40)

check error[unknown-name]: the module `reading` has no function `rounded_up`
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | reading.rounded_up(412, 40)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A private declaration is never exported: no importer reaches it qualified, unqualified, as a pipeline step, or — for a private receiver function — as value.f(). A helper marked private is free to change without changing the module's contract.

docs.title: What private marks
docs.text:
private may mark every declaration a module writes: a function, a receiver function, a type, a trait and a module-level binding.

  • A public declaration may not mention a private type or trait in its signature — a parameter, a result, a bound, a field or a supertype. The checker rejects such a declaration, since an importer would receive a value of a type it cannot name.
  • The parser rejects private on an impl. An implementation of a trait holds in every module that sees the type and the trait.

docs.title: A program is public
docs.text:
A program is read by no other unit, so every declaration in it is public, and the parser rejects private there:

private fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2

double(21)

parse failure[unexpected-token]: `private` belongs to a module: every declaration of a program is public, since no other unit reads it
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | private fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2
  | ^^^^^^^

docs.title: internal is reserved
docs.text:
internal is visibility across the modules of one package: wider than one module, narrower than every importer. It is reserved, and the parser rejects it wherever it is written:

internal fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2

double(21)

parse failure[unexpected-token]: `internal` is reserved: visibility across one package is admitted once every module records its package; mark the declaration `private`, or leave it public
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | internal fn double(n: Int) : Int = n * 2
  | ^^^^^^^^

docs.title: 9. I/O
docs.text: Every program so far read values written into the program itself. This chapter reads files, standard input and the network, writes files and standard output, passes values between parts of a program, and logs what a program does, all through one model: a program reads from a source and writes to a target.

docs.title: Sources and targets
docs.text:
source(endpoint, Format) reads every document an endpoint holds and gives them as values. A source is a value, and a pipeline starts from it the way it starts from a list:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| map(s => s.species)

["wren", "kingfisher"]

Three things meet in that first step, and each has a page. An endpoint, file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), states where bytes are; constructing it performs no I/O. A format, Json, states how the bytes are documents, here one JSON document per line. source joins the two. Whether the documents end is carried by the type of what it gives: a file gives a Seq, standard input a Stream, and the checker reports which steps each one allows.

Writing is the mirror. target(endpoint, Format) writes one completed value as one document, and sink(endpoint, Format) writes one document per value as each arrives:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))
| filter(s => s.seen == "morning")
| map(s => s.species)
| sink(stdout, Text)

wren
kingfisher

Both writing steps give Unit, and a Unit result prints nothing: the two lines above were written by sink while the program ran.

The io module is part of the prelude, so none of this needs an import. Logging and the network are modules of their own, import logging and import net.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text: Page What it covers Endpoints stdin, stdout, stderr, file(p) and file(p).end; Readable, Writable and Replayable; where a relative path resolves Reading with source documents as Data, the format from the extension, reading as a declared record, and the decode error Writing with target and sink one document or one document per value, replace or append, and branches that write Finite or live Seq from a file and Stream from a pipe, tap, and batches with collect(n) Formats and documents what one document reads as, how documents are separated, and which extension implies which format Sources and targets by id [sources.<id>] in hql.toml, the kind that states the type, the schema boundary, and writing by id Channels Channel<T>(name), an endpoint of values held in memory Logging Logger, the five levels, --log-level, and logs kept as values The network http, websocket and socket with import net Effects and what a host allows effectful operations, and what hql eval, hql render and hql check grant hql on the command line hql '<program>', --to, --compact and --from

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
An endpoint of bytes needs a format to make its bytes documents. A channel holds values instead. Channel<T>(name) is an endpoint of values of type T, held in memory for one evaluation. It keeps the values' type, so it takes no format. target writes one value to it, sink writes each value of a sequence, and source gives what it holds now:

c = Channel<Int>("nums")
1 | target(c)
[2, 3] | sink(c)
source(c)

[1, 2, 3]

Values are read in the order they were written. Reading does not consume: two reads give the same values.

c = Channel<Int>("n")
[1] | sink(c)
a = source(c)
b = source(c)
[size(a), size(b)]

[1, 1]

tap(c) gives only what is written after it, as a stream:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
[1] | sink(c)
t = tap(c)
[2] | sink(c)
t | take(5)

[2]

docs.title: The element type is checked
docs.text:
A channel's T is checked as any other type is, and a format beside a channel is a type error, since a channel holds values rather than bytes:

c = Channel<Int>("n")
"x" | target(c)

check error[type-mismatch]: Channel<Int> holds Int, not String
 --> <expression>:2:7
  |
2 | "x" | target(c)
  |       ^^^^^^^^^

c = Channel<Int>("n")
source(c, Json)

check error[type-mismatch]: a channel holds values, not bytes, so it takes no format
 --> <expression>:2:8
  |
2 | source(c, Json)
  |        ^

docs.title: One name, one channel
docs.text:
A channel lives for its execution scope: a program run, or one cell of a document. Within a scope one name is one channel, and constructing the same name with another element type is an evaluation failure naming both:

a = Channel<Int>("n")
b = Channel<String>("n")
1

execute failure[invalid-argument]: the channel "n" holds Int, so it is not also a Channel<String>
 --> <expression>:2:5
  |
2 | b = Channel<String>("n")
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

A cell of a document being rendered may write a channel, because a channel stays inside the evaluation (effects and what a host allows). A channel of LogEvent values is how a program keeps its own logs as values.

docs.title: hql on the command line
docs.text:
With source and sink, hql is a structured-data tool for the shell. A first argument that names no command is a program, so hql '<program>' is hql eval '<program>':

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species)'
"wren"
"kingfisher"

The result is a Stream<String>, so the host writes each value as it arrives, in HQL, the format a result is written in unless --to names another (writing results out).

docs.title: --to and --compact
docs.text:
--to json presents each document of the result pretty-printed, as jq . does, and --compact gives one line each, as jq -c does:

$ head -1 examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json)' --to json
{
  "seen": "dusk",
  "site": "meadow",
  "species": "barn owl"
}

$ head -2 examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json)' --to json --compact
{"seen":"dusk","site":"meadow","species":"barn owl"}
{"seen":"morning","site":"hedge","species":"wren"}

Concatenated JSON values are what source(…, Json) reads, so the output of one hql is the input of the next. sink(e, Json) writes one document per line whatever the flags: a program writing a file says what the file is, and --compact is about the terminal.

Converting between formats is a source and a --to:

$ hql 'source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | map(s => s.site)' --to yaml
- meadow
- hedge
- barn
- river

docs.title: --from
docs.text:
--from names the format of standard input once, on the command line, so the program reads stdin without naming one; a format the program names wins:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql --from json 'source(stdin) | map(s => s.site)'
"meadow"
"hedge"
"barn"
"river"

docs.title: Input and output stay in the program
docs.text:
The command line names no input and no output of a program's own. Input is source or tap in the program, output is target or sink in the program, and --to only chooses how the host writes the final result. A program whose result is Unit prints nothing:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | filter(s => s.seen == "morning") | map(s => s.species) | sink(stdout, Text)'
wren
kingfisher

hql run - reads the program from standard input, so such a program cannot also read stdin as data, and source(stdin, …) in it is a type error. --log-level sets every logger's threshold (logging).

docs.title: Sources and targets by id
docs.text:
A program that names a file path is tied to one machine's files. A vault declares its sources in hql.toml instead, each under an id, and a program names only the id. The field station of the data sources examples is such a vault, and the programs on this page run with --vault examples/sources/station:

[sources.journal]
kind = "vault"
root = "journal"

[sources.counts]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/counts.csv"

[sources.sightings]
kind = "json"
path = "data/sightings.json"

journal = source("journal")
journal.cards | map(c => c.name)

["kite", "owl", "wren"]

A vault is a folder of documents, each a card with a name, the subject of chapter 16; journal.cards is the cards of that one. Here it is one source among others, read by its id like the rest.

docs.title: The kind states the type
docs.text:
source("journal") is a Vault, with its own cards. source("counts") is a Seq<Data>, a row per element, and a json source is the elements of its file's one array:

source("counts")

[{count: "2", species: "wren"}, {count: "1", species: "owl"}, {count: "1", species: "kite"}]

source("sightings") | map(s => s.species)

["wren", "owl", "kite"]

The kinds are vault, csv, json, json_lines, yaml and sqlite, the last one table of a database file. A path resolves against the directory of hql.toml. The type comes from the configuration, so checking a program reads hql.toml and opens nothing else.

A source read as a declared record decodes each element as the record, as a file does, and tap("id") gives a finite source one element at a time, as a Stream:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("counts")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

4

docs.title: The id is a literal
docs.text:
The type of a source is known only from its configuration, so the id is written in the program as a literal, and a connection string is not an id:

id = "counts"
source(id)

check error[type-mismatch]: `source` names a configured source by a literal id, `source("field_notes")`: a computed id would leave its type unknown until evaluation
 --> <expression>:2:8
  |
2 | source(id)
  |        ^^

source("postgres://db/birds")

check error[type-mismatch]: "postgres://db/birds" is not a source id: connection details belong in configuration, `[sources.<id>]` in hql.toml, and a program names the id
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("postgres://db/birds")
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

An id the configuration does not declare is a name error that names the nearest one:

source("count")

check error[unknown-name]: no source `count` is configured; did you mean `counts`?
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source("count")
  |        ^^^^^^^

docs.title: The schema boundary
docs.text:
The names and types an external system uses are facts about that system, not about the program's types, so they are configured beside the source. The station's ledger is a CSV whose headers are Species Name, Total and Observer. [sources.<id>.fields.<field>] maps a field of the record a program reads to its external field, by name for a column or a key, and by a dotted path for a key below the top level of a JSON or YAML document:

[sources.ledger]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/ledger.csv"

[sources.ledger.fields.species]
name = "Species Name"

[sources.ledger.fields.count]
name = "Total"

[sources.profiles]
kind = "json"
path = "data/profiles.json"

[sources.profiles.fields.id]
name = "user_id"

[sources.profiles.fields.name]
path = "profile.display_name"

type Profile {
    id   : String
    name : String
}

profiles : Seq<Profile> = source("profiles")
profiles | map(p => p.name)

["Ada", "Grace"]

A field's table also takes type, the external type where the format's default is not it; absent, the external values read as an absent optional field, an empty cell in CSV unless written; and write = false for a field a write leaves out.

strictness says what a read does with an external field no field of the record reads. It is compatible unless written: the field is passed to the type, so a closed record does not decode a ledger with an Observer column. Under open the field is not read, under warn it is not read and is reported, and under strict it is an error:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

execute failure[io-failure]: source `ledger`: document 1 does not decode as Tally: field `Observer`: Tally declares no such field
 --> <expression>:6:24
  |
6 | tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger")
  |                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

[sources.ledger_open]
kind = "csv"
path = "data/ledger.csv"
strictness = "open"

[sources.ledger_open.fields.species]
name = "Species Name"

[sources.ledger_open.fields.count]
name = "Total"

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("ledger_open")
tallies | map(t => t.count) | sum

4

hql boundary <file> <id> --as <Type> prints a source's effective boundary, each property with the layer it comes from, the format's default or the configuration:

$ hql --vault examples/sources/station boundary tally.hql ledger --as Tally
source ledger (csv), read as Tally; strictness compatible, mode replace
species : String
  external Species Name    configuration
  type     text            format
  position 1               format
  read     true            format
  write    true            format
  absent   empty, missing  format
count : Int
  external Total           configuration
  type     text            format
  position 2               format
  read     true            format
  write    true            format
  absent   empty, missing  format

docs.title: Writing by id
docs.text:
A configured source is also a target. xs | target("id") writes a Table<R>, or a List<R> or Seq<R>, of a declared record R through the same boundary: each field under its external name, in position order, a field with write = false left out. The kind fixes the format, so a format beside the id is a type error, and a vault is read and never written:

type Tally {
    species : String
    count   : Int
}

tallies : Seq<Tally> = source("counts")
tallies | filter(t => t.count > 1) | target("counts")

Unit

source("counts") | target("counts")

check error[type-mismatch]: `target("counts")` writes rows of a declared record, and Data is not one
 --> <expression>:1:20
  |
1 | source("counts") | target("counts")
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

source("counts") | target("counts", Csv)

check error[type-mismatch]: a configured target's format is its kind's, set in its configuration; name none
 --> <expression>:1:20
  |
1 | source("counts") | target("counts", Csv)
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The source's table takes mode, how a write treats what the target already holds. It is replace unless written:

mode A file A SQLite table create written where none exists; an existing file is an evaluation failure created where none exists; an existing table is an evaluation failure append the rows or documents added after the ones held; created where none exists rows inserted; the table created where none exists replace rewritten whole dropped and created again with the rows written

Reading a target the same evaluation has replaced is an evaluation failure, as for a file, and a document being rendered writes nothing (effects and what a host allows).

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
An endpoint states where bytes are. Constructing one performs no I/O: it opens, stats and resolves nothing, and prints as it was written:

file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")

file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")

Four endpoints are bound by the host, as vault is, and need no configuration: stdin, stdout, stderr and file(path).

docs.title: What an endpoint can do is its type
docs.text:
An endpoint's capabilities are its supertypes. A Readable endpoint is read by source and tap, a Writable one is written by target and sink, and a Replayable endpoint is a Readable one that gives the same bytes on every read within one evaluation. Stdin is Readable, Stdout and Stderr are Writable, and File is Replayable and Writable. Reading an endpoint that is not readable is a type error, reported before the program runs:

source(stdout, Json)

check error[type-mismatch]: `source` needs (Readable | String), not Stdout
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | source(stdout, Json)
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The String in the diagnostic is the other form of source, a configured source named by its id (sources and targets by id).

docs.title: A file and its end
docs.text:
file(p) is the whole file. file(p).end is a second endpoint, the end of the same file: Readable and Writable, and not Replayable, since what comes after the end is not there yet. Which endpoint a step names decides what the step does, so a file has no open mode:

file(p) file(p).end source every document in the file, as a Seq a type error naming tap tap the documents one at a time, then it ends the documents appended from now on, as tail -f gives them target, sink replace the file append to the file 
source(file("app.log").end, Lines)

check error[type-mismatch]: the end of a file holds nothing yet; follow what is appended there with `tap`
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source(file("app.log").end, Lines)
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Where a relative path resolves
docs.text:
A relative path resolves against the directory of the source unit that names it: the document for hql render, the program file for hql run, and the working directory for hql eval and the REPL. A document or program reads the same file wherever it is run from. The programs in this chapter run from the repository root, so examples/io/sightings.jsonl is the file in the I/O examples.

A path with a scheme is a type error naming the network endpoint, since a URL is not a file:

file("https://example.com/x.json")

check error[type-mismatch]: "https://example.com/x.json" is a URL, not a file; a network resource is read with `http`
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | file("https://example.com/x.json")
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

The network adds http, websocket and socket with import net, and a channel is an endpoint of values rather than bytes.

docs.title: Finite or live
docs.text:
A file is replayable, so reading it gives a Seq: the documents end, and every step in the book applies. Standard input arrives once, as it is written, so reading it gives a Stream. hql check prints each type:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))

Seq<Data>

source(stdin, Json)

Stream<Data>

That is the difference the streams chapter drew. map, filter and take run over standard input one document at a time, as it arrives. A step that needs the whole input is a type error until the stream is bounded with take(n) or batched with collect(n):

source(stdin, Json) | size

check error[type-mismatch]: `size` needs a finite input, and Stream<Data> may not end; bound it first with `take(n)`, or batch it with `collect(n)`
 --> <expression>:1:23
  |
1 | source(stdin, Json) | size
  |                       ^^^^

The same program checks over a file and over a pipe, and the checker reports which steps each one allows.

docs.title: One document at a time with tap
docs.text:
tap(endpoint, Format) reads any readable endpoint as a Stream, one document at a time, holding only the current one in memory. Over a file, source holds every document and gives a Seq; tap holds one and gives a Stream, so a file larger than memory is read with tap:

tap(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"))

Stream<Data>

tap(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | take(2) | map(s => s.species)

["barn owl", "wren"]

Over a live endpoint the two give the same stream: tap(stdin, Json) is source(stdin, Json). Over a file's end, tap gives each document appended after the tap began, as tail -F does, and waits for a file that does not exist yet:

tap(file("app.log").end, Lines) | take(1)

waits for the next line written to app.log, and gives it.

A format that is one whole document, such as Text, is not read one at a time:

tap(file("examples/io/counts.csv"), Text)

check error[type-mismatch]: Text is one document, so it is not read one at a time; read it whole with `source`
 --> <expression>:1:5
  |
1 | tap(file("examples/io/counts.csv"), Text)
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

docs.title: Batches
docs.text:
collect(n) gathers consecutive values into lists of n, and a list is finite, so a stream is answered in pieces:

tap(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | collect(2) | map(b => b | size) | take(2)

[2, 2]

Written by sink, each batch is one document:

tap(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | map(s => s.species) | collect(2) | sink(stdout, Json)

["barn owl","wren"]
["barn owl","kingfisher"]

Over standard input the same program writes each array as soon as its second value has arrived:

$ cat examples/io/sightings.jsonl | hql 'source(stdin, Json) | map(s => s.species) | collect(2) | sink(stdout, Json)'
["barn owl","wren"]
["barn owl","kingfisher"]

docs.title: What each shape allows
docs.text:
A Seq<T> is a Stream<T> that ends, so every rule for a stream holds for a sequence, and a sequence has more:

Seq<T> Stream<T> that is not a Seq source gives it over a Replayable endpoint or a channel over a live endpoint tap reads it one value at a time reads it as it is target writes one document a type error sink writes one document per element writes one document per value the result, by --to one whole text one piece per value, as it arrives size, sort, xs[i], contains accepted a type error filter, map, take, drop, tee accepted accepted, one value at a time collect(n) gives List<List<T>> gives Stream<List<T>>, in batches

emit keeps its meaning from the streams chapter: it gives the members of each list a stream carries. It is not needed to turn a Seq into a Stream, because a Seq already is one.

docs.title: Formats and documents
docs.text: A format states how bytes are documents: how one document is read from bytes and written to them, and how one document is separated from the next. The formats are the Format types of the writing results out chapter. source and tap decode with them, target and sink encode with them.

docs.title: What one document reads as
docs.text:
Format One document reads as Documents are separated by Json Data whitespace between top-level values Yaml Data a --- line Csv Data, one row keyed by the header a line; the header is read once Lines String, one line without its terminator a line terminator JsonLines Data, one JSON document per line a line terminator Text, Markdown, Hmd, Hql String, the whole text not separable: one document

Lines and JsonLines are framing formats, one document per line. The same file read as Lines gives its lines as strings, and read as Json or JsonLines the documents those lines hold:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Lines) | take(1)

["{\"species\": \"barn owl\", \"site\": \"meadow\", \"seen\": \"dusk\"}"]

A whole-text format reads one document, the whole file:

source(file("examples/io/counts.csv"), Text) | size

1

Bytes that do not decode in their format are an evaluation failure naming the endpoint, the line and the column.

D2 and Mermaid describe a whole, so they are written by target only:

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Mermaid)

check error[type-mismatch]: Mermaid is written, not read
 --> <expression>:1:8
  |
1 | source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl"), Mermaid)
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | sink(stdout, Mermaid)

check error[type-mismatch]: Mermaid describes a whole, so it is written by `target`, not `sink`
 --> <expression>:1:47
  |
1 | source(file("examples/io/sightings.jsonl")) | sink(stdout, Mermaid)
