A value that breaks a rule anywhere along this pipeline stops the program with the failure named. Validation as a value is the form that keeps going.

docs.title: Open and closed types
docs.text: A record type reads a Data tree through tree | T. Whether the type is closed or open decides what the tree may hold besides the fields the type declares.

docs.title: A plain type is closed
docs.text:
type Point = {…} admits exactly its fields. A tree with each of them, at the declared types, reads as a Point:

type Point = {
    x: Int
    y: Int
}

d : Data = {x: 1, y: 2}
d | Point

Point(x = 1, y = 2)

A tree with a field the type does not declare does not read. The refusal is an evaluation failure, since the shape of a Data value is known only when the program runs, and it names the field:

type Point = {
    x: Int
    y: Int
}

d : Data = {x: 1, y: 2, z: 3}
d | Point

execute error[contract-violation]: this does not read as Point: field `z`: Point declares no such field
 --> <expression>:7:1
  |
7 | d | Point
  | ^^^^^^^^^
  = expected: Point

A tree missing a field fails the same way, naming the field that is missing. A closed type is the right one for a value the program owns: the program wrote every field, so a field it did not write is a mistake.

docs.title: A type narrowing Data is open
docs.text:
type User : Data = {…} declares the part of a tree the program relies on. A tree reads as a User when it has those fields; the rest of the tree is kept beneath the view, neither checked nor dropped:

type User : Data = {
    id: String
    name: String
}

d : Data = {id: "u-42", name: "Alice", phone: "+41", country: "CH"}
user = d | User
user.name

"Alice"

The view is static. user.phone is a name error, since User declares no phone, even though the tree holds one. Another view over the same value sees it:

type User : Data = {
    id: String
    name: String
}

type Contact : Data = {
    phone: String
}

d : Data = {id: "u-42", name: "Alice", phone: "+41", country: "CH"}
user = d | User
(user | Contact).phone

"+41"

Typing changed what was known of the value and changed nothing in it. An open type is the right one for data someone else produces: a consumer requires at least these fields, and the producer is free to add others.

docs.title: Optional fields are a separate choice
docs.text:
email?: String is a field that may be absent. It reads as an Option<String>, none where the tree has no entry. It does not make the type open:

type User = {
    name: String
    email?: String
}

xs : List<Data> = [{name: "Alice"}, {name: "Bob", email: "bob@example.com"}]
xs | User | map(u => u.email) | List

[none, "bob@example.com"]

A tree {name: "Alice", phone: "+41"} still does not read as this User: phone is undeclared, and the type is closed. Required against optional is about one field; open against closed is about every field the type does not name.

docs.title: Reading a collection
docs.text:
A step | T over a List<Data>, a Seq<Data> or a Stream<Data> reads each element, and the result is a collection of T. A decoded file is read the same way, one document at a time:

type Sighting : Data = {
    species: String
}

source(file("examples/structural/sightings.jsonl"), Json)
| Sighting
| map(s => s.species)

["barn owl", "wren", "barn owl", "kingfisher"]

Json is the format, and decodes bytes to Data at the source. Sighting is the type, and reads each tree in the pipeline. The format is not a step of its own: | Json | Sighting is not written, because a format is how bytes are read, not a type a value has.

docs.title: Testing before reading
docs.text:
is(T) asks whether a tree reads as T, and of_type(T) keeps the elements that do, at type T, as of_type(Int) kept the integer leaves in chapter 2. Over a Data tree the test is by shape: the declared fields present at their types, and no undeclared one where T is closed.

type Point = {
    x: Int
    y: Int
}

xs : List<Data> = [{x: 1, y: 2}, {x: 1}, {x: 3, y: 4, z: 5}]
[xs | map(d => d | is(Point)), xs | of_type(Point) | map(p => p.x)]

[[true, false, false], [1]]

The second tree lacks y, and the third has a z the closed Point does not declare. is tests structure only; the rules a contract adds are the next two pages, and a contract's rules are held by | T, by its constructor and by validate(T), not by is.

docs.title: Type contracts
docs.text: A contract is a record type with rules. type User : TypeContract = {…} is a closed one: it admits exactly its declared fields, as a plain type does, and every value of it holds every rule written in its body.

docs.title: Rules beside the fields
docs.text:
A rule is written require P, where P is a Bool expression over the contract's fields. A tree reads as the contract when its shape fits and every rule holds:

type User : TypeContract = {
    id: String
    name: String
    age?: Int

    require id != ""
    require name != ""
    require age? >= 0
}

d : Data = {id: "u-42", name: "Alice", age: 34}
d | User

User(id = "u-42", name = "Alice", age = 34)

An optional field is read in a rule as age?, and the rule applies only where the field is present: a tree without age holds require age? >= 0.

A value that breaks a rule does not read, and every broken rule is named as written, in one failure:

type User : TypeContract = {
    id: String
    name: String
    age?: Int

    require id != ""
    require name != ""
    require age? >= 0
}

d : Data = {id: "", name: "Alice", age: -3}
d | User

execute error[contract-violation]: this does not read as User: `require id != ""` does not hold; `require age? >= 0` does not hold
  --> <expression>:12:1
   |
12 | d | User
   | ^^^^^^^^
   = expected: User

Structure comes first: a tree missing a field or holding one at the wrong type fails for that, and no rule runs over it. The rules see a value whose fields all read.

Only a contract has rules. require in a plain type is a type error, and the message names both contract forms.

docs.title: The constructor is held to the rules
docs.text:
A contract built in the program, User(id = …), is checked as a read tree is. A field written age: Int = 18 has a default: where neither the constructor nor the tree gives the field, the default stands, and the rules see it:

type User : TypeContract = {
    id: String
    age: Int = 18

    require id != ""
    require age >= 0
}

[User(id = "u-1"), User(id = "u-2", age = 34)]

[User(id = "u-1", age = 18), User(id = "u-2", age = 34)]

User(id = "", age = -1) fails as d | User fails over the same values, naming both rules. There is no way of making a User that skips its rules, which is what makes the type worth having: a function taking a User needs no check of its own.

A default is a literal of the field's type, a scalar or a list, set or record of literals. It is never a call, and it is written on a required field; an optional field has no default, since absence is its value.

docs.title: Rules a subtype inherits
docs.text:
A record declared under a contract, type Window : Span = {…}, has the fields and the rules of Span and its own, and a rule of Window reads both sets of fields:

type Span : DataContract = {
    low: Int
    high: Int

    require low <= high
}

type Window : Span = {
    width: Int

    require width == high - low
}

d : Data = {low: 1, high: 10, width: 9}
d | Window

Window(low = 1, high = 10, width = 9)

A tree {low: 10, high: 1, width: 9} breaks both: Span's rule and Window's are named together, Span's first.

docs.title: Where a type contract belongs
docs.text: A TypeContract is closed, so it is for values the program is the author of: a canonical record after the data from outside has been read and reshaped, a message the program sends, a value it stores. Every field is accounted for, and every rule is a fact about the value that holds wherever the value goes. The open form, for data the program receives, is the next page.

docs.title: Validation as a value
docs.text: tree | T stops the program at the first value that does not read. A pipeline over many values wants the other answer too: which ones failed, why, and what to do with them. validate(T) gives that as a value.

docs.title: One result per value
docs.text:
d | validate(T) is a Result<T, Invalid>: ok of the value read, or err of one Invalid that holds the original tree and every reason it did not read. A match covers both, and nothing is thrown:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    require id != ""
}

d : Data = {id: ""}
match d | validate(UserData) {
    ok(user) => user.id,
    err(e) => fmt("{} violation of {}", e.violations.size(), e.contract),
}

"1 violation of UserData"

Over a List<Data>, a Seq<Data> or a Stream<Data>, validate(T) is elementwise and keeps the shape: a List<Result<T, Invalid>>, a stream of results. An invalid element is a value in the collection, not an exception out of it. oks() keeps the successes at type T, and errs() keeps the failures at type Invalid:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    age?: Int

    require id != "" as id_present
    require age? >= 0
    warn age? < 120
}

xs : List<Data> = [{id: "u-1", age: 34}, {id: "", age: -3}, {age: "x"}, {id: "u-4", age: 130}]
results = xs | validate(UserData)
[
    results | oks() | map(u => u.id),
    results | errs() | flat_map(e => e.violations) | map(v => v.rule)
]

[["u-1", "u-4"], ["UserData.id_present", "UserData.2", "UserData.id.missing", "UserData.age.type"]]

Four things to see. The second value breaks two rules and both are reported. The third is missing id and has a text age: both structural faults are reported, and no rule ran over it. The fourth breaks only the warning and is among the successes. And every reason has a stable name: a named rule by its name, an unnamed one by its position, a structural fault by its field and kind.

docs.title: What a violation holds
docs.text:
A Violation is a record, not a message. Its contract and path say where, its kind says what sort of fault, missing, type, undeclared or rule, its rule is the stable identity and text the rule as written. For a structural fault, expected holds the declared type and actual the tree the field held:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    age: Int
}

d : Data = {age: "forty-two"}
match d | validate(UserData) {
    ok(_) => [],
    err(e) => e.violations | map(v => [v.rule, v.kind, v.expected | unwrap_or("-"), fmt("{}", v.actual)]),
}

[["UserData.id.missing", "missing", "String", "none"], ["UserData.age.type", "type", "Int", "\"forty-two\""]]

A message is there for display, and a program reads the structured fields instead. Violation and Invalid are themselves open contracts declared in the standard library, so a producer may attach a source or a position, and a failure written to a file reads back with | Invalid.

docs.title: The original value
docs.text:
Invalid.value is the tree as it was validated, before any default was applied. A rejected value carries what is needed to repair it or to replay it later, without a lookup elsewhere:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    age: Int = 18
    require id != "" as id_present
}

xs : List<Data> = [{id: "u-1"}, {id: ""}, {id: "u-3"}, {id: "", age: 3}]
xs | validate(UserData) | errs() | map(e => e.value)

[{id: ""}, {age: 3, id: ""}]

docs.title: Both sides at once
docs.text:
A pipeline that keeps the accepted values and does something else with the rejected ones is a fork: one input broadcast to named branches, each a pipeline of its own. Each result lands on one side, in source order, and each side is an ordinary collection to continue with or to write out:

type UserData : DataContract = {
    id: String
    require id != "" as id_present
}

xs : List<Data> = [{id: "u-1"}, {id: ""}, {id: "u-3"}]
{ accepted, rejected } = xs | validate(UserData) | fork { accepted = oks(), rejected = errs() }
[accepted | map(u => u.id) | json, rejected | map(e => e.violations | map(v => v.rule)) | json]

[[
  "u-1",
  "u-3"
], [
  [
    "UserData.id_present"
  ]
]]

The rejected side written to a sink is a dead letter: the full rejected tree and its violations, as data, where another program reads it back.

docs.title: The policy is the pipeline
docs.text:
The contract says what is valid. What happens to an invalid value is not a setting of the contract; it is the shape of the pipeline around it, and the same contract serves each:

To Write stop at the first invalid value xs \| T keep every result and decide xs \| validate(T) skip the invalid xs \| validate(T) \| oks() keep the accepted, route the rejected xs \| validate(T) \| fork { accepted = oks(), rejected = errs() } accept with a note a rule written warn

Over a stream that does not end the same words hold, and the stream continues past an invalid element as it continues past any other:

type Reading : DataContract = {
    value: Int
    require value >= 0
}

fn readings() : Stream<Data> {
    yield {value: 1}
    yield {value: -1}
    yield {value: 2}
    for r in readings() {
        yield r
    }
}

readings() | validate(Reading) | oks() | map(r => r.value) | take(5)

[1, 2, 1, 2, 1]

validate(T) reads a Data tree or an open view. A value that is already a closed record was checked when it was made, and validate(Point) over a Point is a type error saying so: there is nothing left to find out.

docs.title: Validators
docs.text: A check that several contracts share gets a name. A validator type is a trait whose supertype is Validator, implemented for the type of value it checks with one function, validate(self) : Bool. A contract names it in a rule, or declares a field with it.

docs.title: Declaring one
docs.text:
Email below is implemented for String. The field work_email: Email is a String held to the check as it is read; the rule validate contact? with Email holds the optional contact to the same check, where it is present:

trait Email : Validator { }

impl Email for String {
    fn validate(self) : Bool = self.contains("@") and not self.starts_with("@")
}

type Signup : DataContract = {
    contact?: String
    work_email: Email

    validate contact? with Email
}

d : Data = {work_email: "ada@lovelace.org"}
d | Signup

Signup(contact = none, work_email = "ada@lovelace.org")

Signup.work_email is a String: a field declared with a validator type has the type that implements it. The validator adds a check, not a type of value.

A tree {work_email: "@lovelace.org", contact: "nobody"} breaks both. The failure names the field's check as work_email: Email and the rule as written, validate contact? with Email.

docs.title: A function or a type
docs.text: validate f with V takes either. A function of the field's type to Bool, as is_country_code was on the previous page, is the check written once in the program. A validator type is the check with a name in the type system: a field can be declared with it, a library can export it, and a diagnostic can name it. A validator named in a rule must be implemented for the field's type; validate age with Email over an Int field is a type error naming the missing implementation.

docs.title: The standard validators
docs.text:
import validators brings the standard ones. Email is implemented for String. NonEmpty is implemented for String, text that is more than whitespace, and for List<T>, a list with an element:

import validators

type Signup : DataContract = {
    email: Email
    name: String
    tags: List<String>

    validate name with NonEmpty
    validate tags with NonEmpty as tagged
}

xs : List<Data> = [
    {email: "ada@lovelace.org", name: "Ada", tags: ["math"]},
    {email: "ada@", name: "  ", tags: []}
]
xs | validate(Signup) | map(r => match r {
    ok(s) => s.email,
    err(e) => e.violations | map(v => v.rule) | join(" "),
})

["ada@lovelace.org", "Signup.email Signup.1 Signup.tagged"]

The second signup breaks three checks, and all three are named: the field declared with a validator as Signup.email, the unnamed rule by its position, and the named rule by its name. validate(Signup) is the form that gives these back as a value instead of stopping, and is the next page.

A validator implemented for more than one type, as NonEmpty is, is named in a rule, where the field's type selects the implementation. It cannot be a field's type, since there would be two types to read the field as.

The module is imported by name and never by the prelude, so a program's own Email is its own. It is written in HQL, in lib/std/validators/mod.hql, and a validator of the program's is declared the same way.

docs.title: 12. Errors
docs.text:
A failure is an operation that did not produce the value its signature promises. HQL has two kinds of failure, and each has its own mechanism:

  • A data failure is a value. err(e) of a Result<T, E>, and an Invalid with its Violations, are ordinary values of the program: map, match, errs() and sink act on them as on any other value.
  • A diagnostic is an event. A phase of the run — the loader, the parser, the checker, the planner, the evaluator or the renderer — writes one when it cannot do what the program asked. The program never constructs a diagnostic and never reads one.

The call site determines which of the two a data failure is. x | validate(User) gives Result<User, Invalid>, a value; x | User requires x to read as a User, and a value that does not is a diagnostic of the execute phase. No operation moves a failure from one side to the other.

Term Meaning failure an operation did not produce the value its signature promises data failure a failure the program keeps as a value: err(e), Invalid, Violation diagnostic a structured event describing a failure, written by a phase phase when the diagnostic occurred: load, parse, check, plan, execute, render kind what the problem is, by a stable kebab-case name: type-mismatch, division-by-zero severity how serious it is: debug, info, warning, error, failure disposition what the phase did next: warning, recoverable, fatal diagnostic channel the one Channel<Diagnostic> of a run, which every phase writes into format a rendering of a diagnostic: DiagnosticText, Json target where a rendered diagnostic is delivered: standard error by default

The two pages of this chapter take the sides in turn:

  • Failures as data: Result, validate, Invalid and Violation, and the operations over them.
  • Diagnostics: the four axes, the diagnostic channel, the formats, strict and collect, and the exit status.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Diagnostics are what hql says back. Chapter 13 is the rest of the conversation: the commands, the REPL, the reports and the settings.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: A diagnostic is a structured event a phase of the run writes when it cannot do what the program asked, or has a fact about the program worth stating. It is not a value of the program.

docs.title: The four axes
docs.text:
Every diagnostic has four independent fields, each set by the phase that wrote it:

Axis Values Says phase load, parse, check, plan, execute, render when it occurred kind unexpected-token, unknown-name, type-mismatch, division-by-zero, … what the problem is severity debug, info, warning, error, failure how serious it is disposition warning, recoverable, fatal what the phase did next

The text form is headed by three of them, phase severity[kind]. A parse failure leaves no syntax tree:

[1, 2

parse failure[unexpected-token]: expected `]` after collection elements, found end of input
 --> <expression>:1:6
  |
1 | [1, 2
  |      ^

A check error is found before anything runs:

"total: " + 3

check error[type-mismatch]: `Add` for String takes String, not Int
 --> <expression>:1:13
  |
1 | "total: " + 3
  |             ^

An execute failure depends on a value, so hql check accepts the program and the run fails:

[6, 0, 3] | map(n => 6 / n)

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:1:22
  |
1 | [6, 0, 3] | map(n => 6 / n)
  |                      ^^^^^
  = element: 0, position 2 of 3 in `map`
  = bindings: n = 0

No axis is derived from another. A contract read x | T and a division by zero both fail in the execute phase; the first is an error, a wrong value read, and the second a failure, an operation with no result. An integer literal outside the Int range is a numeric-overflow of the parse phase, and the same kind in the execute phase is an addition whose sum left the range.

docs.title: Fields beyond the axes
docs.text:
What a field carries is not repeated in the message. Under the caret, the text form shows one = line per field that applies:

  • cell: the cell of a document the diagnostic is about;
  • note: a second place in the source, with what is there;
  • help: what to write instead, a nearest name or a conventional spelling;
  • expected and found: the type a step needed, and what was there;
  • element: the element a step was applying its function to;
  • source: the document a card the failure was about was read from;
  • bindings: the parameters in scope where it failed;
  • trace: the functions it was reached through, outermost first.
[1, 2] | mapp(n => n)

check error[unknown-step]: `mapp` is not a pipeline step
 --> <expression>:1:10
  |
1 | [1, 2] | mapp(n => n)
  |          ^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: did you mean `map`?

trait Shape { fn area(self) : Float }
type Circle { radius : Float }
impl Shape for Circle { fn area(self) : Float = 3.0f }
impl Shape for Circle { fn area(self) : Float = 4.0f }
1

check error[duplicate-implementation]: `Shape` is already implemented for Circle: a trait has one implementation per type
 --> <expression>:4:1
  |
4 | impl Shape for Circle { fn area(self) : Float = 4.0f }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = note: the first implementation, at <expression>:3:1

A failure inside called functions names each call that reached it, and the parameters of the function it is in:

fn ratio(total: Int, parts: Int) : Int = total / parts

fn share(xs: List<Int>) : Int = ratio(xs | sum, size(xs) - 3)

share([4, 5, 6])

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:1:42
  |
1 | fn ratio(total: Int, parts: Int) : Int = total / parts
  |                                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = bindings: parts = 0, total = 15
  = trace: share (call) → ratio (call)

A failure over a card's value names the document the card was read from. Here the divisor is zero for the book of 112 pages:

cards
| filter(c => c.metadata.category == "book")
| map(c => match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => 1000 / (n - 112), _ => 0 })

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:3:52
  |
3 | | map(c => match c.metadata.pages { some(Int n) => 1000 / (n - 112), _ => 0 })
  |                                                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = element: "a-room-of-ones-own", position 1 of 7 in `map`
  = source: books/a-room-of-ones-own.hmd

docs.title: The diagnostic channel
docs.text:
A run owns one diagnostic channel, Channel<Diagnostic>. It is a channel as the channels page of chapter 9 describes one: typed, in memory, its values in the order they were committed. Two properties set it apart. Its scope is the run, not one evaluation: it is opened before the loader reads the vault and closed after the last phase, so a parse failure or a type error, written before any HQL is evaluated, has a channel to go to. And the program holds no name for it: no operation reads the channel of the run it is in.

Every phase writes into it in order. A check warning and an execute failure of one run arrive in that order, and the failure leaves the warning intact:

fn totalOf(xs : List<Int>) : Int = xs | sum

totalOf([1, 2, 3]) / 0

check warning[naming-convention]: `totalOf` is a function, written in snake_case
 --> <expression>:1:1
  |
1 | fn totalOf(xs : List<Int>) : Int = xs | sum
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = help: write it `total_of`

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | totalOf([1, 2, 3]) / 0
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

2 diagnostics: 1 failure, 0 error, 1 warning

The loader writes into the same channel. A document whose header does not parse is skipped with a load warning[skipped-document], and the rest of the vault is read. A warning never changes the exit status.

docs.title: Formats and targets
docs.text:
What the channel holds reaches a person or a tool through a format and a target. The default is DiagnosticText on standard error, with the value on standard output. The host's options change that wiring, not the program:

Option Effect --diagnostics-format json each diagnostic is one JSON document per line on standard error, every field that applies present --envelope json one JSON document on standard output: the type, the value, and the channel's contents under diagnostics --report-level LEVEL the lowest severity shown; a hidden diagnostic is still in the channel and in the envelope 
"total: " + 3

{"disposition":"fatal","kind":"type-mismatch","message":"`Add` for String takes String, not Int","origin":"<expression>","phase":"check","severity":"error","span":{"end":13,"start":12}}

A report is the channel's contents rendered in a format, followed by a count per severity when there is more than one. It names a presentation, not an object of the run.

docs.title: Diagnostics as data in a later run
docs.text:
A run never reads its own channel, and a later run reads what an earlier one delivered as it reads any data. Diagnostic is a record of the standard library, so a file written with --diagnostics-format json reads back with | Diagnostic, and DiagnosticText writes such records as the report a run prints, without the source line:

source(file("run.jsonl"), JsonLines)
| Diagnostic
| filter(d => d.severity == "error" or d.severity == "failure")
| format(DiagnosticText)

execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> examples/error-handling/diagnostics/warning-then-failure.hql

docs.title: Continuation: strict and collect
docs.text:
Whether a phase continues after a diagnostic is the phase's. --report collect asks every phase for as much continuation as it can give; strict, the default, declines optional continuation after the first error.

Phase After an error Under collect load skips the document and continues the same parse stops: nothing after an unparseable source has a structure the same check stops at the first checks every statement; a failed one still binds its name plan stops: a refused pipeline has no plan the same execute stops at the first map steps past an element whose function failed; an overflow or an I/O failure stops under both render stops at the failing cell renders every cell, each reported against its own fault

Under collect, the element map stepped past is lost, the value stands without it, and the diagnostic says disposition: recoverable:

$ hql --report collect '[6, 0, 3] | map(n => 6 / n)'
[1, 2]
execute failure[division-by-zero]: division by zero
 --> <expression>:1:22
  |
1 | [6, 0, 3] | map(n => 6 / n)
  |                      ^^^^^
  = element: 0, position 2 of 3 in `map`
  = bindings: n = 0

The value is on standard output and the diagnostic on standard error. In --diagnostics-format json the same diagnostic carries "disposition": "recoverable"; under strict it is fatal and there is no value.

The exit status is 1 when the channel holds a diagnostic at or above error, and 0 otherwise. The run above produced a value and still exits 1: a failure was written.

docs.title: The lifecycle of a fatal diagnostic
docs.text:
A fatal diagnostic ends its phase, and later phases do not start. What was written before it stays in the channel, and the run ends only after the channel's delivery consumers have delivered everything written:

Delivering a diagnostic never resumes the computation. Handling a failure is done with data, on the other side of the model.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: This is the last chapter. The examples page lists the runnable programs in the repository, the error-handling cases among them.

docs.title: Failures as data
docs.text: A data failure is a value of the program. Its type says it may be a failure, the checker holds every use of it to that type, and the run writes no diagnostic for it.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Result<T, E> is ok(v) or err(e). A function that may fail declares it in its result type, and a match covers both cases:

fn parse(text: String) : Result<Int, String> = match text.to_int() {
    some(n) => ok(n),
    none => err(fmt("not a number: {}", text)),
}

["4", "x", "15"] | map(parse)

[ok(4), err("not a number: x"), ok(15)]

A Result is not its value. parse("4") + 1 is a type error, found before anything runs:

parse("4") + 1

check error[type-mismatch]: addition requires two Int, two Float or two Decimal operands, or two values of a type implementing `Add`, not Result<Int, String>
 --> <expression>:7:1
  |
7 | parse("4") + 1
  | ^^^^^^^^^^

unwrap_or gives the value or a default, map_err changes the error, and oks() and errs() keep one side of a sequence of results:

results = ["4", "x", "15"] | map(parse)
{
    total: results | oks() | sum,
    rejected: results | errs(),
    fallback: parse("x").unwrap_or(0),
}

{fallback: 0, rejected: ["not a number: x"], total: 19}

docs.title: validate: a contract read as a value
docs.text:
x | validate(T) reads x as the declared type T and gives Result<T, Invalid>. An Invalid carries the contract, the value and one Violation per broken rule, each with its path, kind, expected and actual:

type User { name : String, age : Int }

{name: "bob", age: "forty"} | validate(User)

err(Invalid(contract = "User", value = {age: "forty", name: "bob"}, violations = [Violation(contract = "User", path = ["age"], kind = "type", rule = "User.age.type", text = "\"forty\" is not Int", expected = "Int", actual = "forty", severity = "error", message = "field `age`: \"forty\" is not Int")]))

Over many rows, errs() keeps the rejected ones as data the program can count, sort or write out:

type User { name : String, age : Int }

rows = [{name: "ada", age: 36}, {name: "bob", age: "forty"}]
rows
| map(row => row | validate(User))
| errs()
| map(invalid => invalid.violations | map(v => v.message))

[["field `age`: \"forty\" is not Int"]]

The run above writes no diagnostic, and its exit status is 0. A Violation with severity = "warning" is data in the same way.

docs.title: x | T: a contract read as a requirement
docs.text:
Without validate, x | T requires x to read as T. A value that does not is a failure of the execute phase, written as a diagnostic, and the run ends:

type User { name : String, age : Int }

Data("{\"name\": \"bob\", \"age\": \"forty\"}", Json) | User

execute error[contract-violation]: this does not read as User: field `age`: "forty" is not Int
 --> <expression>:3:1
  |
3 | Data("{\"name\": \"bob\", \"age\": \"forty\"}", Json) | User
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  = expected: User

The diagnostic carries the same Violations validate would have given, as its context. They remain the diagnostic's: no operation reads them back into the program. Which of the two forms to write is the program's decision, at the call site: validate where a rejected value is part of the result, | T where it ends the run.

docs.title: What is next
docs.text: Diagnostics describes the other side: what a diagnostic carries, where it goes, and when a run stops.

docs.title: Commands at a glance
docs.text:
Command What it does hql eval <program> check and evaluate an argument hql check <file> print the type without evaluating hql run <file> check and evaluate a file hql repl read, evaluate and print, keeping bindings hql render <file> run the HQL cells in a document and build the Markdown document they yield hql help <name> the declarations of a function, type, trait or module, with their doc strings hql builtins list the steps hql config the reporting mode and shown level in force, and where each came from hql doctor check the semantic-search chain and name the first missing part hql ai list the model requests waiting under --ai host, and answer one (next release)

hql '<program>' is hql eval '<program>'. - reads standard input wherever a file is taken. Success is exit 0, a language or I/O failure 1, a usage error 2.

docs.title: Doc strings
docs.text: A block of /// lines opened after an empty line is the doc string of the declarations below it, up to the next empty line. hql help <name> and :help <name> in hql repl print each declaration of a name with its module and doc string; :type <name> prints the first sentence. The pages below are the standard library's doc strings, one page per function, type and trait.

docs.title: The standard library
docs.text:
• std/core — The types every other module is written in: the scalars, the collection types, the open tree Data, absence, failure, value order, the format category and the core traits.
  • std/doc — Documents: a header of everything known about one and a body someone wrote, and the card, a document a vault holds.
  • std/retrieval — Retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query.
  • std/graph — Graphs: nodes and the edges among them, structural only; what a node or an edge means is the knowledge module's.
  • std/knowledge — Knowledge: the semantic domain, where everything is a claim.
  • std/collections — The operations over the collection types core declares: membership, filtering, mapping, order, grouping, joins and reductions.
  • std/string — The functions of a String, in the prelude.
  • std/seq — The sequence, set and map operations beyond the core's membership, order and lookup, in the prelude.
  • std/math — Numbers, in the prelude.
  • std/option — The ways out of an Option<T>, in the prelude, each stating what absence gives.
  • std/result — The ways out of a Result<T, E>, in the prelude, each stating what a failure gives.
  • std/regex — Text matched against a regular expression.
  • std/format — The formats, how bytes are read as values and how values are written as text, and the codec contracts over them.
  • std/io — Input and output: endpoints, the data sources read from them, and the data targets written to them.
  • std/io/net — Network endpoints: transports, read and written by source, tap, target and sink like any other endpoint (module io).
  • std/io/logging — Logging: structured events written to a destination, apart from the result.
  • std/vault — The current vault: the source a program runs against.
  • search/lexical — Lexical retrieval: a corpus ranked by the words it shares with a query, a hashed bag of words compared by cosine.
  • search/semantic — Semantic retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query by vectors a language model made ahead of time, read from the index that [semantics] index in hql.toml names.
  • std/validators — Validators: the standard validator types, imported where they are used, import validators, and never by the prelude, so a program's own Email is its own.

docs.title: search/lexical
docs.text:
module lexical

Lexical retrieval: a corpus ranked by the words it shares with a query, a hashed bag of words compared by cosine. Offline, deterministic and exact; it models no meaning, so a query and a document that share no word score zero. Imported where it is used: import lexical.

  • lexical — Lexical retrieval: a corpus ranked by the words it shares with a query, a hashed bag of words compared by cosine.

docs.title: lexical
docs.text:
In search/lexical.

fn lexical<T : Doc>(self: Collection<T>, query: String) : Ranking<Card>

The cards of self ranked by the words their text shares with query, as a Ranking<Card>. The text of each, and query, is a hashed bag of its words of two or more letters or digits, lowercased, and the two are compared by cosine. A card that shares no word with query scores zero and is not a hit; the rest are in descending order of score. The retrieval names the model hql.hashbag.v1 and the metric cosine, and is not approximate.

docs.title: search/semantic
docs.text:
module semantic

Semantic retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query by vectors a language model made ahead of time, read from the index that [semantics] index in hql.toml names. The query is looked up in the index too; one the index does not hold is an evaluation failure. Imported where it is used: import semantic.

  • semantic — Semantic retrieval: a corpus ranked against a query by vectors a language model made ahead of time, read from the index that [semantics] index in hql.toml names.

docs.title: semantic
docs.text:
In search/semantic.

fn semantic<T : Doc>(self: Collection<T>, query: String) : Ranking<Card>

The cards of self ranked against query by the cosine of their vectors in the vault's index, as a Ranking<Card> in descending order of score; a card scoring zero or less is not a hit. query must be in the index. A card the index holds no vector for is left out of the ranking, with a warning; one changed since the index was built is scored, with a warning that its score is stale.

docs.title: std/collections
docs.text:
module collections

The operations over the collection types core declares: membership, filtering, mapping, order, grouping, joins and reductions. Each one is callable directly or as a pipeline step, and carries the shape a planner splits it by.

  • Group — One partition of a group: its key, and the occurrences with that key in input order, as items.
  • size — The number of element occurrences in self, an Int: [1, 2, 2, 3] | size is 4, and Set([1, 2, 2]) | size is 2.
  • count — The number of element occurrences in self, as size gives it: count is the kept alias of size.
  • contains — true when value occurs in self, and false otherwise: [1, 2, 3] | contains(2) is true.
  • get — The value a map holds for key, or none when the key is missing: {"a": 1} | get("a") is 1, and {"a": 1} | get("b") is none.
  • filter — The elements for which a type test holds, each at the tested type.
  • of_type — The elements whose runtime type is type or one of its subtypes, each at that type, in an F<U>: filter(x => x | is(U)).
  • is — true when the runtime type of self is type or one of its subtypes.
  • somes — The present values of a collection of options, in an F<T>; the absent ones are dropped: [some(1), none, some(3)] | somes is [1, 3].
  • oks — The success values of a collection of results, in an F<T>; the failures are dropped: [ok(1), err("x"), ok(3)] | oks is [1, 3].
  • errs — The error values of a collection of results, in an F<E>; the successes are dropped: [ok(1), err("x"), ok(3)] | errs is ["x"].
  • map — Each element through by, in a collection of the input's constructor: [1, 2, 3] | map(x => x * 10) is [10, 20, 30].
  • retry — Each element through the fallible operation, invoked again while it fails with an error when accepts (every error, without when) and fewer than attempts invocations have run.
  • take — The first n elements.
  • drop — The elements after the first n, in the input's order and type: [5, 3, 4] | drop(1) is [3, 4].
  • collect — Consecutive elements in batches of n, in order; the last batch may be shorter: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] | collect(2) is [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]].
  • emit — Every member of every sequence, in order, the inverse of collect: [[1, 2], [3]] | emit is [1, 2, 3].
  • flat_map — Each element through by to a sequence, and the members of those sequences in order: map(by) | emit.
  • sort — The elements in ascending order: by their own value order, by the key by gives each, or by a comparison by of two elements.
  • group — The occurrences partitioned by the key by gives each, as a set of Groups, each a key and its occurrences in input order.
  • join — The pairs of an element of the input and an element of other that match, each built by into, ordered by the input element's position, then other's.
  • left_join — A join that keeps every element of the input: one with no match in other is built by into with none on the right.
  • right_join — A join that keeps every element of other: one with no match in the input is built by into with none on the left.
  • full_join — A join that keeps every element of both sides, with none for the missing side; the unmatched elements of other come after the matched results.
  • cross_join — Every pair of an element of the input and an element of other, built by into, in order, with no condition: [1, 2] | cross_join(["a", "b"], into = (x, y) => [x, y]) is [[1, "a"], [1, "b"], [2, "a"], [2, "b"]].
  • semi_join — The elements of the input that match some element of other, by keys, a predicate on, or both; each is kept at most once, in its position.
  • anti_join — The elements of the input that match no element of other, by keys, a predicate on, or both, in their positions.
  • reduce — The elements folded from the left by by, from initial, or without it from the first element, the result then none over []: [1, 2, 3] | reduce(0, (a, x) => a + x) is 6.
  • sum — The sum of the occurrences, reduce(0, +); [] | sum is 0.
  • product — The product of the occurrences, reduce(1, *); [] | product is 1.
  • average — The mean of the occurrences, or none over []: [1, 2] | average is 1.5.
  • merge_all — Every map merged in order, a later key winning: reduce({:}, merge).
  • union_all — Every member of every set: reduce(Set([]), union).
  • concat_all — Every member of every sequence, in order: reduce([], concat).
  • min — The least occurrence by value order, reduce(min), or none over [].
  • max — The greatest occurrence by value order, reduce(max), or none over [].
  • variance — The population variance of the occurrences, as a Float, or none over []: [1, 2, 3, 4] | variance is 1.25.
  • count_by — The number of occurrences with each key by gives, as a map from key to count; empty over [].
  • histogram — The number of occurrences in each bucket of width, keyed by the bucket's lower bound, the greatest multiple of width not above the value, in key order: [1, 5, 12, -3] | histogram(5) is SortedMap {-5: 1, 0: 1, 5: 1, 10: 1}.
  • top_k — The k greatest occurrences, by value order or by the key by gives, greatest first, equal keys in input order: [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] | top_k(2) is [5, 4].
  • approx_distinct — An estimate of the number of distinct occurrences, size(Set(xs)); 0 over [].

docs.title: approx_distinct
docs.text:
In std/collections.

reduction fn approx_distinct<T>(self: Collection<T>) : Int

An estimate of the number of distinct occurrences, size(Set(xs)); 0 over []. The estimate is deterministic: the same input gives the same result.

docs.title: average
docs.text:
In std/collections.

reduction fn average(self: Collection<Int>) : Option<Float>
reduction fn average(self: Collection<Float>) : Option<Float>
reduction fn average(self: Collection<Decimal>) : Option<Decimal>

The mean of the occurrences, or none over []: [1, 2] | average is 1.5. Ints and Floats average to a Float; a Decimal mean is the sum divided by the count, as Decimal / divides.

docs.text:

fn collect<T>(self: Collection<T>, n: Int) : List<List<T>>

Consecutive elements in batches of n, in order; the last batch may be shorter: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] | collect(2) is [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]. n is at least 1. xs | collect(n) | emit is xs.

docs.title: count
docs.text:
In std/collections.

reduction fn count<T>(self: Collection<T>) : Int

The number of element occurrences in self, as size gives it: count is the kept alias of size. [1, 2, 2, 3] | count is 4.

docs.title: count_by
docs.text:
In std/collections.

reduction fn count_by<T, K>(self: Collection<T>, by: T -> K) : Map<K, Int>

The number of occurrences with each key by gives, as a map from key to count; empty over []. ["a", "bb", "c"] | count_by(s => size(s)) is Map {1: 2, 2: 1}.

Every pair of an element of the input and an element of other, built by into, in order, with no condition: [1, 2] | cross_join(["a", "b"], into = (x, y) => [x, y]) is [[1, "a"], [1, "b"], [2, "a"], [2, "b"]].

docs.title: drop

fn drop<S : Iterable<T>, T>(self: S, n: Int) : S

The elements after the first n, in the input's order and type: [5, 3, 4] | drop(1) is [3, 4]. The checker rejects an input without a stable order, such as a Set.

docs.text:

fn is<T, U>(self: T, type: Type<U>) : Bool

true when the runtime type of self is type or one of its subtypes. The checker rejects a test no T can pass, and warns about one every T passes. Used as a filter predicate, it narrows the result.

docs.title: join
docs.text:

fn join<T, U, K, R>(self: Seq<T>, other: Seq<U>, *, left: T -> K, right: U -> K, on: (T, U) -> Bool, into: (T, U) -> R) : Seq<R>

docs.title: map
docs.text:
In std/collections.

elementwise fn map<F<_> : Iterable<_>, T, R>(self: F<T>, by: T -> R) : F<R>
elementwise fn map<T, R>(self: Option<T>, by: T -> R) : Option<R>
elementwise fn map<T, R, E>(self: Result<T, E>, by: T -> R) : Result<R, E>

Each element through by, in a collection of the input's constructor: [1, 2, 3] | map(x => x * 10) is [10, 20, 30]. A Set maps to its image, which may hold fewer elements than the input. Over an Option, by applies to a present value and none stays none; over a Result, by applies to the success value and a failure is unchanged.

docs.title: std/core
docs.text:
module core

The types every other module is written in: the scalars, the collection types, the open tree Data, absence, failure, value order, the format category and the core traits. A type sits here when a module below it would otherwise import a module above it: Data is a tree of sequences and maps, so the collection types are core types, and the operations over them are the collections module's.

  • Orderable — A type whose values have a total order: of any two values of the type, one comes first or the two are equal.
  • Scalar — A leaf: a value with no parts of its own.
  • Bool — The truth values true and false: a Scalar with equality and no order.
  • Int — A 64-bit whole number, ordered by value: 7 / 2 is 3, and 7 % 2 is 1.
  • Float — A 64-bit binary floating-point number, written with the suffix f (2.5f), ordered by value.
  • Decimal — An exact decimal number, written with a decimal point and no suffix (2.50), ordered by value: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is true.
  • String — Text, ordered character by character: "ab" + "cd" is "abcd", and "hello"[1] is "e".
  • Date — A calendar date, ordered by time.
  • Iterable — A value whose elements can each be visited: the bound an operation states when it only visits each value.
  • Collection — A finite multiset of occurrences, unordered, with no runtime representation.
  • Stream — An ordered, possibly unending run of values x0, x1, x2, ....
  • Seq — A finite stream: a collection in which every occurrence has exactly one position in 0 .. size(c) - 1.
  • List — A sequence of materialized occurrences; repeated traversal preserves positions.
  • Set — Materialized distinct values under HQL equality: count(s, x) <= 1.
  • Map — Materialized associations from distinct keys of K to values of V; not a Collection.
  • OrderedMap — A Map whose keys keep their construction positions: its keys are a Seq<K>.
  • SortedMap — An OrderedMap whose key positions follow the intrinsic total order of K.
  • Data — An open tree whose keys belong to whoever wrote them: what a YAML or JSON document is.
  • TypeContract — The supertype of a closed contract: a structural type declared type C : TypeContract = {…} has exactly its declared fields, and is validated as a contract.
  • DataContract — The supertype of an open contract: a structural type declared type D : DataContract = {…} is a view over Data with at least its declared fields, and is validated as a contract.
  • Option — An optional value of T: present, holding one T, or absent.
  • Result — A computation that may have failed: ok(value) with a T, or err(error) with an E.
  • Ordering — The result of compare(a, b): Less, Equal or Greater.
  • Type — A type written as an argument: is(Card), of_type(Card).
  • Format — The category of formats: how bytes are documents.
  • Is — What a predicate that tests its parameter's type, x => x | is(U), gives: a Bool that, where true, holds the parameter at U.
  • Eq — Equality: a == b and a != b over a type implementing Eq call its eq.
  • Ord — Order: a < b and the other comparisons over a type implementing Ord call its compare.
  • Add — Addition: a + b over a type implementing Add is a.add(b).
  • Sub — Subtraction: a - b over a type implementing Sub is a.sub(b).
  • Mul — Multiplication: a * b over a type implementing Mul is a.mul(b).
  • Div — Division: a / b over a type implementing Div is a.div(b).
  • Rem — Remainder: a % b over a type implementing Rem is a.rem(b).
  • Range — A window of positions, what a slice takes: xs[a:b] is xs[Range(start = a, end = b)], and a bound left out is absent.
  • Index — A position: xs[i] over a type implementing Index is xs.at(i), the element there or its absence.
  • Slice — A part: xs[a:b] over a type implementing Slice is xs.slice(Range(start = a, end = b)), a value of the type itself.
  • Validator — A check a value passes: a trait extending Validator is a validator type.
  • Operation — A function from I to O that also carries its shape: what an executor may assume about splitting the step.
  • Elementwise — An Operation whose result for each element depends on that element alone, so it may run over any split of its input: map and filter are elementwise.
  • Partition — An Operation that regroups its input by a key, each group running independently and completing in any order: group is one.
  • Reduction — An Operation that collapses its whole input to one value through a combiner the runtime holds, so each split may be reduced and the results combined: size combines by addition, contains by disjunction.
  • Barrier — An Operation that needs its whole input before any output, so it is not split: sort, take and reduce are barriers.
  • Pair — Two values held together, each at its own type: what zip, enumerate, entries and join produce, and what Pair(first = a, second = b) builds.
  • Violation — One reason a value does not read as a contract, as validate(T) reports it.
  • Invalid — A value that did not read as a contract, and every reason why: its contract, the value, and the violations.
  • Diagnostic — A diagnostic a run delivered, read back as data: its phase, kind, severity and disposition, its message, and where it points, origin and span, a {start, end} byte range.

docs.title: Collection
docs.text:
In std/core.

abstract type Collection<T> : Iterable<T>

A finite multiset of occurrences, unordered, with no runtime representation. size(c) is the number of occurrences, count(c, x) the number equal to x, and contains(c, x) holds where count(c, x) > 0; so size(c) is the sum of count(c, x) over the distinct values in c.

docs.text:
In std/core.

An open tree whose keys belong to whoever wrote them: what a YAML or JSON document is. It is a union of exactly three alternatives: a Scalar leaf, a sequence of trees, or a String-keyed map of trees.

fn Data<F : Format>(text: String, as: Type<F>) : Data

text parsed in the format as: Data("[1, 2]", Json) is [1, 2], and s | Data(Yaml) is one call. The format is one whose decoder reads Data: Json, JsonLines, Yaml or Csv. A framed format, JsonLines or Csv, gives the list of its records; Json or Yaml gives one document. Text that does not parse fails at run time.

Where a document is and what it is called are facts about the file, so they are fields of the document itself, and nothing in the header or the metadata can contradict them. docs.title: std/format
docs.text:
module format

The formats, how bytes are read as values and how values are written as text, and the codec contracts over them.

A format is a type narrowing Format, the category core declares. It names an external representation and, where it applies, its framing: Lines is text framed one record per line, JsonLines one JSON document per line. A format is not the text it encodes, so none narrows String, and it is not Format<T>, since one format encodes many value structures. Whether what is read ends is a property of the source, not of the format: source(file(p), Lines) is a Seq<String> and source(stdin, Lines) a Stream<String>.

A String is always UTF-8. Every format that holds text reads and writes UTF-8, and decoding bytes that are not UTF-8 is a decoding error.

  • Text — The plain-text format: read, the whole input is one String; written, a value is its display text, and a String its characters as they are.
  • Lines — The format of text framed one record per line: read, each line is one String; written, each element of a collection is one line: [1, 2] | lines is "1 2".
  • Hql — The format of HQL's own value notation: {a: 1, b: [true]} | hql is "{a: 1, b: [true]}".
  • Markdown — The Markdown format: read, the whole input is one String; written, a collection is a list, one item per element: [1, 2] | markdown is "- 1 - 2".
  • Hmd — The HyperMarkDown format, a narrowing of Markdown: every HyperMarkDown text is Markdown, and a value is written in it as in Markdown.
  • Json — The JSON format: read, each document is one Data value; written, a value is one indented JSON document.
  • JsonLines — The JSON Lines format, one JSON document per line: read, each line is one Data value; written, each element of a collection is one line of compact JSON: [{a: 1}, {a: 2}] | jsonlines is "{"a":1} {"a":2}".
  • Yaml — The YAML format: read, each document of the input, --- separating them, is one Data value; written, a value is one YAML document.
  • Csv — The comma-separated values format, with a header row: read, each row is one Data value whose fields, named by the header, hold Strings; written, a collection of records or a Table is the header and one row per element.
  • D2 — The D2 diagram format, which writes a Graph, or a Data value holding one, and nothing else.
  • Mermaid — The Mermaid diagram format, which writes a Graph, or a Data value holding one, and nothing else.
  • DiagnosticText — The text form of a Diagnostic (HQL-0045), which writes a diagnostic, or a sequence of them, and nothing else: each one's heading, phase severity[kind]: message, its origin and the fields that apply, then a count per severity when there is more than one.
  • Table — Rows of type R under ordered columns: the shape every format's encoder writes as a table.
  • Decoder — The contract that a format's records are read as values of T: source(e, F) gives the T of F's decoder.
  • Encoder — The contract that values of T are written as records of a format: format(x, F) takes the types F's encoders cover.
  • format — The formats, how bytes are read as values and how values are written as text, and the codec contracts over them.
  • text — x encoded as Text: x | text is format(x, Text).
  • hql — x encoded as Hql: x | hql is format(x, Hql).
  • markdown — x encoded as Markdown: x | markdown is format(x, Markdown).
  • hmd — x encoded as Hmd: x | hmd is format(x, Hmd).
  • json — x encoded as Json: x | json is format(x, Json).
  • yaml — x encoded as Yaml: x | yaml is format(x, Yaml).
  • csv — x encoded as Csv: x | csv is format(x, Csv).
  • lines — x encoded as Lines: x | lines is format(x, Lines).
  • jsonlines — x encoded as JsonLines: x | jsonlines is format(x, JsonLines).
  • d2 — x encoded as D2: x | d2 is format(x, D2).
  • mermaid — x encoded as Mermaid: x | mermaid is format(x, Mermaid).

docs.title: std/graph
docs.text:
module graph

Graphs: nodes and the edges among them, structural only; what a node or an edge means is the knowledge module's. There is no Node type: what a node is arrives as a type parameter, so a graph over documents and a graph over concepts share one declaration.

  • Edge — An edge from source to target, with data about it.
  • Graph — A graph: the set of its nodes, which are cards, and the set of its edges, the links among them.
  • Link — An authored link from one document to another: an Edge between cards.
  • HmdGraph — The document graph: a Graph of cards and the authored Links among them.
  • uplinks — The edges of the links x writes to other cards: one Edge per authored link, its source the card x.
  • downlinks — The edges of the links other cards of the vault write to x: one Edge per authored link, its target the card x.
  • expand — The graph reached from x by following links depth steps, 1 unless given, in direction: "uplinks", "downlinks" or "both", the default.

docs.title: downlinks
docs.text:
In std/graph.

fn downlinks(x: Option<Doc>) : List<Edge>
fn downlinks(x: Doc) : List<Edge>
fn downlinks(x: Hit<Card>) : List<Edge>

The edges of the links other cards of the vault write to x: one Edge per authored link, its target the card x. Over a hit, the card it holds; over an absent card, none; over a collection, every element's, in order. It needs a vault: a document alone has nothing that points at it.

The graph reached from x by following links depth steps, 1 unless given, in direction: "uplinks", "downlinks" or "both", the default. A depth of 0 is a type error when it is a literal and an evaluation failure when it is computed: Graph(xs) is the graph with no traversal. It needs a vault.

The edges of the links x writes to other cards: one Edge per authored link, its source the card x. Over a hit, the card it holds; over an absent card, none; over a collection, every element's, in order.

docs.title: Edge
docs.text:
In std/graph.

type Edge<S, T> { source : String target : String data : Data }

An edge from source to target, with data about it. Whatever S and T are, each end is held as the name of the node it is.

docs.title: Graph
docs.text:
In std/graph.

type Graph<N, E> { nodes : Set<Card> edges : Set<Edge> }

A graph: the set of its nodes, which are cards, and the set of its edges, the links among them. Both are sets: discovering a graph does not order it. vault.graph is every card of the vault and the links among them.

fn Graph(xs: Graph) : Graph

xs itself: a graph projects to itself.

fn Graph(xs: Collection<Doc>) : Graph
fn Graph(xs: Collection<Hit<Doc>>) : Graph

The graph of the cards in xs, or the cards its hits hold, as nodes, with the vault's edges among them. A relation card is not a node: its source and target are. Graph(vault.cards) has the nodes and edges of vault.graph.

The graph of nodes, together with the source and target of every edge in edges, and the edges as given.

docs.title: std/io
docs.text:
module io

Input and output: endpoints, the data sources read from them, and the data targets written to them. An endpoint names where bytes are and performs no I/O; a format type (module format) states how the bytes are documents; a source or target joins the two, and Seq and Stream state whether the documents end.

  • Endpoint — The abstract type of every endpoint: where bytes are.
  • Readable — An endpoint bytes can be read from, by source and tap.
  • Replayable — A Readable endpoint that gives the same bytes on every read in one evaluation, so source reads what it holds as a Seq.
  • Writable — An endpoint bytes can be written to, by target and sink.
  • Stdin — The program's standard input, bound as stdin: read once, as it arrives.
  • Stdout — The program's standard output, bound as stdout: written while the program runs, before the host presents its result.
  • Stderr — The program's standard error, bound as stderr: where diagnostics go, apart from the result.
  • FileEnd — The end of a file, after what it holds, as file(path).end: a write there appends, and tap follows what is written next, as tail -f does.
  • File — A local file, the whole of it: read, every document it holds; written, it is replaced.
  • Channel — An endpoint of values rather than bytes, held in memory for one execution scope: a program run, or one cell.
  • DataSource — What a program reads: a configured source by id, or an endpoint read in a format.
  • FiniteSource — A source of every document, in order, that ends: read from a Replayable endpoint.
  • LiveSource — A source of each document as it arrives, with no replay: read from a live endpoint.
  • KeyedSource — A finite source whose contents are addressable by a key of type K.
  • Position — A message's place in its log, ordered as the log is.
  • Message — One element of a stream with where and when it sits in it: its value, its position, an optional key and time, and its headers.
  • StreamSource — A log: Message<T>s in order, replayable within its retention.
  • Catalog — An endpoint that contains sources of type S: a database of tables, a cluster of topics.
  • VaultSource — A vault as a source: an endpoint that holds its cards, as a catalog holds tables, with its members as fields rather than names.
  • DataTarget — What a program writes to: an endpoint written in a format, or a configured target by its id.
  • file — The File at path.
  • source — Every document read from endpoint in format, decoded to T: a Seq from a Replayable endpoint, a Stream from a live one.
  • tap — The documents read from endpoint in format, one held at a time, as a Stream<T>.
  • target — Writes value as one document to endpoint in format, or to the target configured under id, and gives Unit.
  • sink — Writes each of values to endpoint in format, one document per value, and gives Unit: [{a: 1}, {a: 2}] | sink(stdout, Json) writes {"a":1} and {"a":2} on two lines.

docs.title: file
docs.text:
In std/io.

fn file(path: String) : File

The File at path. Constructing it is pure and opens nothing: file("birds.json").path is "birds.json". A URL is a type error when it is a literal and an evaluation failure when it is computed; a network resource is read with http.

docs.title: sink
docs.text:
In std/io.

effectful fn sink<T, F : Format>(values: Iterable<T>, endpoint: Writable, format: Type<F>) : Unit

Writes each of values to endpoint in format, one document per value, and gives Unit: [{a: 1}, {a: 2}] | sink(stdout, Json) writes {"a":1} and {"a":2} on two lines. Written to a Channel<T>, each value is appended and no format is taken. Effectful: it runs once, where it is written.

docs.title: source
docs.text:
In std/io.

effectful fn source<F : Format, T>(endpoint: Readable, format: Type<F>) : Iterable<T>
effectful fn source<F : Format, T>(id: String, format: Type<F>) : Iterable<T>

Every document read from endpoint in format, decoded to T: a Seq from a Replayable endpoint, a Stream from a live one. T is the type the format decodes to, or the element type the read is expected to give: s : Seq<Sighting> = source(file("birds.json")) decodes each document as a Sighting. The format may be omitted when the endpoint is file of a literal path whose extension implies one. source(id) reads the source configured under the literal id in hql.toml, as the type its kind states, and takes no format; source(c) of a Channel<T> is a Seq<T> of what it holds now. Effectful: it runs once, where it is written.

docs.title: tap
docs.text:
In std/io.

effectful fn tap<F : Format, T>(endpoint: Readable, format: Type<F>) : Stream<T>
effectful fn tap<F : Format, T>(id: String, format: Type<F>) : Stream<T>

The documents read from endpoint in format, one held at a time, as a Stream<T>. A format that is one whole document, such as Text, is a type error. tap(id) gives the elements of the finite source configured under id as a Stream; tap(c) of a Channel<T> gives each value as it is written; tap(file(path).end, F) follows what is appended. Effectful: it runs once, where it is written.

docs.title: target
docs.text:
In std/io.

effectful fn target<T, F : Format>(value: T, endpoint: Writable, format: Type<F>) : Unit
effectful fn target<T, F : Format>(value: T, id: String, format: Type<F>) : Unit

Writes value as one document to endpoint in format, or to the target configured under id, and gives Unit. A Seq is one document, in Json an array; a Stream that is not a Seq is a type error: write it with sink, or bound it with take(n) first. Written to a Channel<T>, value is appended and no format is taken. Effectful: it runs once, where it is written.

docs.title: std/io/logging
docs.text:
module io.logging

Logging: structured events written to a destination, apart from the result. A logger owns no writer: it names a producer and holds a destination, as sink would write it (module io): stderr or a file in a format, a network endpoint, or a Channel<LogEvent> that keeps the events as values for the host. A program imports the module: import logging.

  • LogLevel — How severe an event is.
  • Trace — The least severe LogLevel, below Debug.
  • Debug — The LogLevel above Trace and below Info.
  • Info — The LogLevel above Debug and below Warn; a logger's threshold unless written.
  • Warn — The LogLevel above Info and below Error.
  • Error — The most severe LogLevel, above Warn.
  • LogEvent — One logged event: its level, the logger that produced it, its message and its data.
  • Logger — A producer of events: its name and the least severe level it writes.
  • trace — Writes one Trace event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is Trace, and gives Unit.
  • debug — Writes one Debug event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Debug, and gives Unit.
  • info — Writes one Info event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Info, and gives Unit.
  • warn — Writes one Warn event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Warn, and gives Unit.
  • error — Writes one Error event with message and data to log's destination, whatever log's threshold, and gives Unit.
  • Cell — The cell hql render is running, bound as cell.

docs.title: debug
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

effectful fn debug(log: Logger, message: String, data: Data = {:}) : Unit

Writes one Debug event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Debug, and gives Unit. Effectful: log | debug("parsed", {rows: 3}).

docs.title: error
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

effectful fn error(log: Logger, message: String, data: Data = {:}) : Unit

Writes one Error event with message and data to log's destination, whatever log's threshold, and gives Unit. Effectful: log | error("unreadable", {path: "birds.json"}).

docs.title: info
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

effectful fn info(log: Logger, message: String, data: Data = {:}) : Unit

Writes one Info event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Info, and gives Unit. Effectful: with log = Logger(stdout, Text, name = "birds"), log | info("loaded", {count: 312}) writes INFO birds loaded {count: 312}.

docs.title: trace
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

effectful fn trace(log: Logger, message: String, data: Data = {:}) : Unit

Writes one Trace event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is Trace, and gives Unit. Effectful. Called directly or through a pipe: trace(log, "step") is log | trace("step").

docs.title: warn
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

effectful fn warn(log: Logger, message: String, data: Data = {:}) : Unit

Writes one Warn event with message and data to log's destination when log's threshold is at most Warn, and gives Unit. Effectful: log | warn("no sightings").

docs.title: Cell
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

type Cell { logs : Channel<LogEvent> }

The cell hql render is running, bound as cell. The events written to its logs are shown beside the cell's result and never saved into the document.

docs.title: Debug
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

type Debug : LogLevel

The LogLevel above Trace and below Info.

docs.title: Error
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

type Error : LogLevel

The most severe LogLevel, above Warn.

docs.title: Info
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

type Info : LogLevel

The LogLevel above Debug and below Warn; a logger's threshold unless written.

docs.title: LogEvent
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

type LogEvent { level : LogLevel logger : String // the producer's name, dotted by convention: hql.query message : String data : Data // structured context, {:} when none is given }

One logged event: its level, the logger that produced it, its message and its data. Written as Text it is one line, the level, the logger and the message, then the data as an HQL literal unless it is empty:

INFO birds loaded {count: 312}

Written as Json it is one document with these four keys.

docs.title: LogLevel
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

abstract type LogLevel

How severe an event is. The five levels are ordered from least to most severe: Trace, Debug, Info, Warn, Error. A level is tested with e.level | is(Error), and a threshold is passed as a type: level = Info.

docs.title: Logger
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

type Logger { name : String level : LogLevel // the least severe level it writes }

A producer of events: its name and the least severe level it writes. Its destination is not a field: what a logger writes to is visible only where it is constructed.

fn Logger<F : Format, L : LogLevel>(to: Writable, format: Type<F>, *, name: String, level: Type<L> = Info) : Logger

A Logger named name that writes to to in format each event at least as severe as level, Info unless written. The format is omitted for a Channel<LogEvent>, which takes the events as values. Construction is pure and writes nothing: Logger(stderr, Text, name = "birds").

docs.title: Trace
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

type Trace : LogLevel

The least severe LogLevel, below Debug.

docs.title: Warn
docs.text:
In std/io/logging.

type Warn : LogLevel

The LogLevel above Info and below Error.

docs.title: std/io/net
docs.text:
module io.net

Network endpoints: transports, read and written by source, tap, target and sink like any other endpoint (module io). Constructing one sends nothing: the request a program describes happens when a source, tap, target or sink uses it, and only if the host grants the network to that program. A document reaches no network. A program imports the module: import net.

  • Http — An HTTP resource at url.
  • WebSocket — A WebSocket connection to url: each message is a document, read as it arrives and written as it is sent.
  • Socket — A TCP connection to host on port.
  • http — The HTTP resource at url, as an Http endpoint: method is the request a write sends, "GET" unless given, and headers a map of header names to values sent with every request.
  • websocket — The WebSocket at url, as a WebSocket endpoint.
  • socket — The TCP endpoint host on port, as a Socket.

docs.title: http
docs.text:
In std/io/net.

fn http(url: String, method: String = "GET", headers: Data = {:}) : Http

The HTTP resource at url, as an Http endpoint: method is the request a write sends, "GET" unless given, and headers a map of header names to values sent with every request. Constructing it sends nothing.

docs.title: socket
docs.text:
In std/io/net.

fn socket(host: String, port: Int) : Socket

The TCP endpoint host on port, as a Socket. Constructing it opens no connection.

docs.title: websocket
docs.text:
In std/io/net.

fn websocket(url: String) : WebSocket

The WebSocket at url, as a WebSocket endpoint. Constructing it opens no connection.

docs.title: Http
docs.text:
In std/io/net.

type Http : {Replayable, Writable} { url : String method : String // "GET" unless written headers : Data // a map of header names to values }

An HTTP resource at url. Read, it is a GET whose response body is its bytes; the host reads it once per evaluation, so it is Replayable. Written, it is a request by method whose body is the document, and the response is not read beyond its status. Both send headers, a map of header names to values. Authentication belongs in a configured source, not in the program.

docs.title: Socket
docs.text:
In std/io/net.

type Socket : {Readable, Writable} { host : String port : Int }

A TCP connection to host on port. A socket carries bytes, not messages, so the documents on it are separated as their format separates them: whitespace between Json values, a line for Lines, JsonLines and Csv, a --- line for Yaml.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
In std/io/net.

type WebSocket : {Readable, Writable} { url : String }

A WebSocket connection to url: each message is a document, read as it arrives and written as it is sent.

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type Catalog<S> : DataSource

An endpoint that contains sources of type S: a database of tables, a cluster of topics.

docs.title: Channel
docs.text:
In std/io.

type Channel<T> : {Readable, Writable} { name : String }

An endpoint of values rather than bytes, held in memory for one execution scope: a program run, or one cell. It holds T, so it takes no format, and its values are read in the order they were written. One name is one channel within a scope.

fn Channel<T>(name: String) : Channel<T>

The channel named name in the current scope, holding T. The element type is written at the call, Channel<LogEvent>("logs"), since nothing written to the channel yet determines it.

docs.title: DataSource
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type DataSource

What a program reads: a configured source by id, or an endpoint read in a format. Its contract fixes what its contents are.

docs.title: DataTarget
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type DataTarget

What a program writes to: an endpoint written in a format, or a configured target by its id.

docs.title: Endpoint
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type Endpoint

The abstract type of every endpoint: where bytes are. Constructing one opens, stats and resolves nothing.

docs.title: File
docs.text:
In std/io.

type File : {Replayable, Writable} { path : String end : FileEnd // file(p).end appends, and tap(file(p).end, F) follows }

A local file, the whole of it: read, every document it holds; written, it is replaced. A relative path resolves against the directory of the source unit that names it: the document, the program file, or the working directory for an expression.

docs.title: FileEnd
docs.text:
In std/io.

type FileEnd : {Readable, Writable} { path : String }

The end of a file, after what it holds, as file(path).end: a write there appends, and tap follows what is written next, as tail -f does. It is live, not Replayable, so source of it is a type error.

docs.title: FiniteSource
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type FiniteSource<T> : {DataSource, Seq<T>}

A source of every document, in order, that ends: read from a Replayable endpoint.

docs.title: KeyedSource
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type KeyedSource<K, T> : FiniteSource<T>

A finite source whose contents are addressable by a key of type K.

docs.title: LiveSource
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type LiveSource<T> : {DataSource, Stream<T>}

A source of each document as it arrives, with no replay: read from a live endpoint.

docs.title: Message
docs.text:
In std/io.

type Message<T> { value : T position : Position key? : Data time? : Date headers : Data }

One element of a stream with where and when it sits in it: its value, its position, an optional key and time, and its headers.

docs.title: Position
docs.text:
In std/io.

type Position : Orderable

A message's place in its log, ordered as the log is.

docs.title: Readable
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type Readable : Endpoint

An endpoint bytes can be read from, by source and tap.

docs.title: Replayable
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type Replayable : Readable

A Readable endpoint that gives the same bytes on every read in one evaluation, so source reads what it holds as a Seq.

docs.title: Stderr
docs.text:
In std/io.

type Stderr : Writable

The program's standard error, bound as stderr: where diagnostics go, apart from the result.

docs.title: Stdin
docs.text:
In std/io.

type Stdin : Readable

The program's standard input, bound as stdin: read once, as it arrives.

docs.title: Stdout
docs.text:
In std/io.

type Stdout : Writable

The program's standard output, bound as stdout: written while the program runs, before the host presents its result.

docs.title: StreamSource
docs.text:
In std/io.

abstract type StreamSource<T> : {DataSource, Stream<Message<T>>}

A log: Message<T>s in order, replayable within its retention.

docs.title: VaultSource
docs.text:

module knowledge

Knowledge: the semantic domain, where everything is a claim. Every declaration is a type; the module declares no operation.

  • Concept — Something identified or described: the type that puts a card in a node position.
  • Proposition — A claim that can be supported, disputed or constrained.
  • Evidence — Material offered for or against a claim.
  • Knowledge — The universe of concepts, relations, propositions and evidence.
  • Relation — A meaningful relation from source to target: an Edge narrowed with identity, evidence and provenance.
  • ConceptCard — A card whose subject is a concept: a Card that is a Concept, and so a node.
  • RelationCard — A card whose subject is a relation: one whose metadata declares knowledge.type: Relation, with a knowledge.relation.source and target that each name a card of the vault.
  • KnowledgeGraph — A graph whose nodes are concepts and whose edges are relations, which is still Knowledge: the projection loses neither contract.

docs.title: std/math
docs.text:
module math

Numbers, in the prelude. abs, pow and sign take an Int or a Float, and abs and sign a Decimal too; round takes a Float or a Decimal, and the rest take a Float. float, int and decimal convert between the three, since no number widens on its own except an Int beside a Decimal.

  • abs — self without its sign, at its own type: abs(-3) is 3, and abs(-1.50) is 1.50.
  • pow — self raised to exponent, both of one type: pow(2, 10) is 1024.
  • sign — -1, 0 or 1 by the sign of self, as an Int: sign(-0.5) is -1.
  • float — self as a Float, the Float nearest it: float(1.10) is 1.1.
  • int — The integer part of self, as an Int, the fraction dropped toward zero: int(-2.9f) is -2.
  • decimal — self as a Decimal: an Int exactly, and a Float by the shortest digits that read back as it: decimal(0.1f) is 0.1.
  • gcd — The greatest common divisor of self and other, at least 0: gcd(12, 18) is 6, and gcd(0, 0) is 0.
  • sqrt — The square root of self: sqrt(2.0f) is 1.4142135623730951.
  • floor — The greatest whole number not above self, as a Float: floor(-1.5f) is -2.0.
  • ceil — The least whole number not below self, as a Float: ceil(-1.5f) is -1.0.
  • round — The whole number nearest self, as a Float; a value halfway between two rounds away from zero: 2.5f | round is 3.0.
  • exp — e raised to self: exp(1.0f) is 2.718281828459045.
  • ln — The natural logarithm of self: ln(1.0f) is 0.0.
  • log10 — The base-10 logarithm of self: log10(1000.0f) is 3.0.
  • sin — The sine of self, an angle in radians: sin(0.0f) is 0.0.
  • cos — The cosine of self, an angle in radians: cos(0.0f) is 1.0.
  • tan — The tangent of self, an angle in radians: tan(0.0f) is 0.0.
